speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

I should like to bring to the attention of the government a matter of urgent general interest to the general public. In the New York Times of March 12, its Washington correspondent makes this announcement.
More effective governmental supervision of radio communication, including authority to defeat attempts to monopolise the ether, was recommended to the House Committee on Merchant Marine to-day by Herbert Hoover, Secretary of Commerce.
Secretary Hoover, in his address, gave his approval to the purposes of the pending White bill, which aims to prohibit monopoly of radio communication, allowing the Interstate Commerce Commission to review the rates charged for such service and laying down drastic regulations governing the issuance of licenses by the Secretary of Commerce for the operation of broadcasting stations.
Is such provision for the protection of the public being made by the government of Canada? I would ask the acting Prime Minister (Mr. Graham) to let the public know whether any proposal looking to a monopoly of radio communication has been made in Ottawa.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Acting Prime Minister): The question of radio is not only new, but intricate, and I would not care to give an answer offhand. As a matter of law and of practice, the management of radio is in the hands of a branch of the Marine department. Licenses are issued; regulations are in force at the present time; inspection takes place; and a small fee is paid, of course, largely for the purpose of paying for this inspection. There has been communication, whether it has been of late or not, between the governments as to the proper control of radio, as there have been or are likely to be so many broadcasting stations that the conflict of the air waves interferes with proper communication.
On the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret very much to have to rise to a question of privilege. I have observed in an address given by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. d'Anjou) in this House on the 10th instant, words which attribute to me language as respects which I want to make contradiction.
I will read or attempt to read the exact language of the hon. member as it appears at page 197 of Hansard:
Le chef de 1'Opposition ne veut pas se rappeler qu'il a ete le principal insulteur de notre province et de notre race et que les partisans qui se tenaient a ses cotes fai-saient la meme sale besogne. Qu'il n'oublie pas une chose: les electeurs de la province de Quebec, toujours fideles a leur devise, se souviennent. Ils se souvien-dront qu'au cours de la Grande Guerre si nous avons connu des jours de tristesse et de deuil nous les devons au chef de l'Opposition et a son parti; ils se souvien-dront, d'autre part, qu'ils peuvent avoir confiance au chef du parti liberal, l'honorable premier ministre, qui a su garder son bon sens alors que presque tous ses compatriotes perdaient la tete pendant la guerre, et qui, fidele a ses principes, 6tant Canadien avant tout, a su se ranger aux cotes de ceux qui voulaient prot^ger leur pays avant de ddfendre l'Empire.
I have read all, that the context might be seen and no injustice done. I will read the translation as I make it:
The leader of the opposition does not wish to recall that he has been the principal insulter of our province and of our race and that the partisans who cling to his side engaged in the same dirty work. Let him not forget one thing: the electors of the province of Quebec, always faithful to their motto "Remember". They will remember that in the course of the great war if we experienced days of sadness and of mourning we owe it to the leader of the opposition and to his party. They will remember, on the other hand, that they can have confidence in the leader of the Liberal party, the hon. Prime Minister, who has preserved his good sense when almost all his compatriots lost their heads during the war, and who, faithful to his principles, being a Canadian before all else, has ranged himself on the side of those who desire to protect their country before defending the Empire.
It is to the first feature alone that I have a right to refer on this occasion, that which ascribes to me an insult to the province of Quebec and to the French-Canadian race. I only desire to say that no words of mine were ever spoken or can be found uttered in this House or out of this House in my entire public or, indeed private life, that afford the slightest foundation for the grave, and I had almost said, base, allegation of the hon. member for Rimouski. This denial I have made repeatedly, and in the whole carnival of calumny on this question no one has ever attempted to substantiate the allegation, so far as I have ever seen, by quotation from my words. The next is more brief:
Le chef de l'opposition semble vouloir agir de la meme fagon que sir John-A. Macdonald; il vient dans notre province flagorner notre clerg6 apres 1'avoir fait insulter.
The leader of the opposition seems to wish to adopt the same methods as Sir John A. Macdonald; he come3 into our province to toady to our clergy after having insulted them.
I can scarcely find words to describe this language. My only right, however, is to deny the allegation as I now do in the strongest possible terms. I can hardly conceive the type of mind which would ascribe that conduct to any person without the slightest foundation in fact. One more sentence:

Hudson Bay Railway
II a oublie qu'il fait partie de cette ligne de fanati-ques qui travaillent a rabaisser autant que possible 1'element canadien-frangais et qui tachent d'ecraser tous ceux qui ne partagent pas leurs opinions.-
He has forgotten that he is a member of that league of fanatics who labour to crush as far as possible the French-Canadian element, and who seek to wipe out all those who do not agree with their opinions.
I do not know what league is referred to.
If the hon. member would be more specific my denial could also be equally specific. I only say that I am a member of no league at all, either in this country or in any other, nor am I a member of any secret society, neither am I a member of any order, nor have I ever been.
BANFF PARK WATER POWER On the Orders of the Day:
Can the Minister of the Interior (Mr. StewarO inform the House what action if any has been taken with respect to the application for water power privileges in the Banff National Park?

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is before the department an application on behalf of the Calgary Power Company, but nothing has been done in the matter; no definite conclusion has been arrived at.
RUSSIAN TRADE DELEGATES On the Orders of the Day:

Does the government's reception of
the trade delegates from Soviet Russia mean the recognition of the Soviet Republic? Does the recognition by England of Soviet Russia involve recognition by Canada?

No.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Acting Prime Minister):	That is a large constitutional
question, which I think will be referred later to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). At this moment the gentlemen to whom my hon. friend refers are in this building. I have had a conversation with them and with some of my colleagues have received the delegates and discussed trade matters with them. As to recognition of Soviet Russia, I do not know what such recognition on the part of England means so far as Canada is concerned; but in relation to the question of trade, I can only say that we are doing business on our own hook.
HUDSON BAY RAILWAY On the Orders of the Day:

I want to call the attention of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) to an editorial that appears in the Montreal Gazette of to-day in which Mr. A. E. Warren, general manager of the Canadian National Railways, western region, is reported as stating that the Minister of Railways has ordered full speed ahead on the Hudson Bay railway. Is this statement correct, and has such an order been given?
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals):	I am glad that my
hon. friend has called my attention to this matter because the definition of the phrase "full speed" may not be fully understood.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) has defined what that means.

I am afraid this definition might not answer this query. Last year, as hon. gentlemen will remember, a certain sum was voted to rehabilitate or to repair and put in operating condition a certain portion of the Hudson Bay railway that has deteriorated during the past few years The estimate having gone through the House late, as nearly all estimates do under our system, very little of that money was expended. I had a conversation with Mr. Warren the other day concerning the matter with a view to taking some steps to expend a certain amount of money that I proposed to put in the estimates, and I believe the Canadian National Railways would be justified in proceeding with the work as soon as possible, trusting to the estimate going through the House.

Consideration of the motion of Mr. Kelly for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his Speech at the opening of the session, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Sutherland, resumed from Thursday, March 13.
The Address-Mr. Lapointe

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I desire first of all to offer my
congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Address. These hon. gentlemen had a fine document to comment upon and I think they have availed themselves splendidly of that opportunity. I may remark also, before I go further, how pleased I am and the members of the government are at the manner in which the Speech from the Throne has been received by the country.
By Brantford?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I expected that; I shall come to the point in a moment. The Speech from' the Throne has received the commendation of all friends of progressiveness and of those who desire to uphold in Canada liberal ideas, liberal principles and liberal policies.
There is still a suspicion over here.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
On the other hand, it
has been criticised by those who belong to a different school. Let me confess to my hon. friends opposite that there are some expressions of approval which I would rather not receive because they would cause me to doubt the correctness of my own line of action. My hon. friends need not point to any member on this side. I am not aware that any supporter of the government has said that he is going to vote against the Address; quite the contrary. I am not surprised at the disappointment of my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) and his associates. The announcements made by His Excellency in his Speech, including the promise of a balanced budget at the end of the present fiscal year, are a decisive answer to the campaign which they have been waging throughout the country during the last six months. The citadel of misrepresentation, so industriously built up by speakers and writers in that pen-and-mouth disease which has raged throughout Canada-that citadel has crumbled. My right hon. friend in his speech on the Address-which was clever, as are all his speeches-obviously expressed the policy of his party, but it was singularly uninspiring. His speech was great in small things, and small in great things. What ray of hope is set before the eyes of young Canadians; what spirit of confidence did he place in their minds and hearts; what message of faith did he deliver to them? Nothing, Sir; nothing but dismay and bitterness. The right hon. gentleman, trying to throw ridicule on the Speech from the Throne, said it was a
IMr. Cardin.]
collection of hopes. Well, if we contrast his own speech with the Speech from the Throne, I am sure we shall all agree that it was an accumulation of discouragement and despair. Unwittingly he has paid a compliment to his opponents. Yes, the Speech from the Throne is a message of faith, of confidence, of life, of progress. The world is moving-I know my hon. friends will smile at that; the mere mention of the word liberalism gets on the nerves of those gentlemen-the world is moving, and we as a young country must move with it, we must set our vision towards the rising sun; looking at the past will not be of much avail.

You are looking
West.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Politically, west, south,
east and north-we on this side of the House are not sectionalists. Social, economic and political systems are clashing in the world today as were the armies on the battlefields five years ago. The victory will rest with those who properly protect and safeguard the needs and rights of the masses, of the producers and of the labouring men. But, Sir, in that battle, as in its counterpart of five years ago, the victory will not side with those who merely use defensive tactics and refuse to move forward.
What constructive statement can be found in the utterances of my right hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, delivered in this House the other day? Apart from unfair depreciation of his opponents, what did it contain? What remedy did he offer, what suggestion did he make? I ask any hon. member and I ask the people of this country, where can they find a constructive suggestion in the speech of my right hon. friend? But I am not surprised at the absence of anything constructive. At a banquet tendered to him last year by his followers in the House of Commons and the Senate, he announced that this will be his policy for some time.
I do not want to be unfair to my right hon. friend, I quote his own words -as reported in the Ottawa Journal of April 18, 1923:
I never can be moved from the discharge of that duty, continued Mr. Meighen, by the importunities of those who think otherwise, by the impatience of a section of the press, nor by any device, however resourceful. I am confident that a foundation of distrust in this administration must be laid by convincing the public that the whole of the past Liberal campaign was dishonest from the beginning.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I knew I would strike
the heart of my right hon. friend. He continued :

The Address-Mr. Lapointe
As soon as we get that conviction general we shall have the foundation on which later constructive policies may be successfully built. That is our first duty, and towards that we have to concentrate our efforts.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
So my right hon. friend
agrees still with that statement of his, that his only duty is to lay a foundation of distrust in the government of the day, and then later, when he shall have been successful, will be the time for constructive policies. Mr. Speaker, no other public man in Canada ever expressed such a statement.
And he has kept his pledge. The sole object of the campaign which has been conducted throughout the country during the last few months has been to hamper the work of those who have to clear up the ghastly muddles and messes which he and his friends have bequeathed to his successors,-what you, Sir, a lover of the classics would call damnosa hereditas. Of course, he has been supported in this campaign by all those who hate liberalism, particularly because they distrust and despise the people. He has been helped by those who are seeking more privileges and know that they cannot get them from the democratic government which is now in power. Read certain speeches, analyze certain statements that have been made, and you will see that this propaganda was a curtain-raiser for a demand for higher protection. The President of the Ontario Liberal-Conservative Association, in Hamilton the other day, when organizing a branch there, said:
We are organizing to chase from Ottawa this terrific-tar iff-cutting government which is in power.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friends say, " hear, hear," but not very long ago they voted for a motion of the right hon. leader of the opposition which declared that we had broken our pledges in that we had not made any reduction in the tariff. I confess that I admire that Tory consistency.
Is the trade of Canada declining? Is failure going to be the outcome of Canadian industry and enterprise? Amid the confusion that has been created in the public mind by lugubrious utterances concerning the things that are hampering our prosperity, there is at least one fact that furnishes solace and courage and ground for a sane judgment on the situation, and that is that our production is increasing all the time and that the national wealth is larger than it ever was. Mr. Speaker, the statistics show that our national wealth is great, and Canadians should
not slander their country-indeed, some of them are even slandering themselves for the purpose of achieving some selfish interest. The statistics show that the trade of Canada has enormously increased; that, as I have said, it has never been larger than it is today. Our exports are greater, and the balance is in our favour. Every time a domestic loan is floated, either by this government or by the provinces, there is money in Canada to subscribe to it. My right hon. friend said the other day that the number of business failures resulting in bankruptcy was increasing; I have here the statistics to show they have decreased fifty per cent during the last year. And yet the "whisperers of death," the disgruntled politicians, and the seekers of privileges, are claiming that all this means nothing and are adducing arguments to prove that the more trade the less wealth, the more exports the less prosperity. My right hon. friend devoted one hour of his time the other day to setting forth such an argument. Imagine what he would say if the figures were the other way.
Reference has been made to the fact that a number of our population have left the country. It is unfortunate that it should be so, but I do not hesitate to say that if men are leaving this country, those who are primarily responsible for it are the whisperers of death, the preachers of blue ruin, the men who say that Canada is to-day a land of desolation, taxes and debts. The young Canadians of to-day will never forgive those who have been slandering their country. I say that Canada and Canadians should be grateful to Providence for the condition in which our country finds itself compared with that of other nations of the world after the crisis which, in common with those other nations, we have gone through. The conditions in Europe are still affecting us. If there is one thing which the war and its effects have taught the people of the world more clearly than anything else it is the interest that every country has in the social and economic life of every other country. We are all interrelated peoples, as individuals, and what does injury to one country does injury to all the countries. Problems which are international in their scope cannot be easily remedied by purely national solutions. That is why I am a strong advocate of a league of nations. Unfortunately, the world is not yet at peace; far from it. Such a prudent and distinguished statesman as Lord Grey of Falloden said at Bath only the other day that he felt it his duty to tell his hearers that things were going from bad to worse in Europe and were shaping, if not

The Address-Mr. Lapointe
immediately, almost certainly, toward another war. From this side of the Atlantic we must certainly say that we do not see any great improvement on the other side. Peace has not resumed its sway over the hearts and minds of men. Stability of currency, which is so necessary to the rebuilding of the shattered fabric of international trade, is not yet apparent. We have seen recently the Belgian franc, the French francs, the German mark, the Russian rouble, suffer fantastic declines; and the same thing has happened in most of the European countries and even in some parts of South America. Canada is standing the test with flying colours, in spite of the whisperers of death. We should be proud of it; we should be grateful to Providence for it, and we should not recriminate as some gentlemen have done for the last few months. I am pleased to see that they seem to realize the error of their ways: for the last few days we have not heard much about our awful financial condition; we have heard only about the tariff. My hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) who is a fine speaker-none better, from the parliamentary viewpoint, in this House-applied himself during the whole of his speech yesterday to the tariff and merely to that. He implored me to convert my speech into a budget speech, because he asked me to give him the details. Let me tell my hon. friend that in his address he was not as logical as he usually is. He said that nothing should be stated in the Speech from the Throne concerning the tariff. Of course this has been done before.
He did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Nothing explicit, he said. Am I right now?

I stated that it was not according to constitutional procedure in this House to anticipate the budget in the Speech from the Throne by declaring any specific reductions in duties on particular articles or classes of articles.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And yet my hon. friend, having stated that it is against constitutional authority or practice to declare in the Speech from the Throne what will be the specific measures with respect to the tariff, has asked me to give him that in detail.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Well, my hon. friend was addressing himself to every one of the ministers.
I asked for an explanation of an ambiguous clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He says that it should
not be specific, and that we should make it still more specific.
After the harm is done.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Then he turned in the
direction of my Progressive friends to his left and warned them that nothing would be done. So it is not explicit, as my hon. friend says.
The other fault he had to find with the government-I do not know whether it is a great fault-was that on two occasions this debate has come very close to an end and to the taking of a vote and my hon. friend was horrified at the prospect of a vote being taken on the amendment. Why, in the press, even in newspapers supporting my hon. friend, we see complaints that this debate is much too long, that it is costing the country $30,000 a day-by the way, while I mention that figure, which I see repeated in all the newspapers of the land, may I say that it is wrong.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
May I at least remove
that sin from the conscience of my hon. friends opposite. I am informed that the real cost to the country of a session of parliament is $55,000 per month, because the rest of the expenditure is spread over the whole year whether there is a session or not. So $30,000 a day is a little too much.
Though it may please my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre, than whom I have no better friend, I really cannot agree to make a budget speech to-day, and I shall speak of something else. The details he is so anxious to receive will be officially given in the budget speech which will be delivered in a few weeks.
May I address myself now for a little while to some statements which have been made by the leader of the opposition in the country, some of which he has repeated in this House? My right hon. friend has carried on a campaign in Canada. We have been pleased to see him in my own province. He made a fine pilgrimage through the province of Quebec, in the course of which we were pleased to see him distribute medals to the schools, colleges and convents. But we were not so pleased to see him distribute misrepresentations of facts to the rest of the people of the province. He frequently at his meetings repeated what I had stated with regard to the net debt of Canada, that the net debt of Canada per capita was lower than the debt of Great Britain and of the other British Dominions. My right hon. friend agreed with that, but then he asked:	"Why does

The Address-Mr. Lapointe
not Mr. Lapointe then say why our taxes are higher?" My right hon. friend asks me a difficult question when he asks me to give the reason, for the simple reason that I cannot find a cause for an effect which exists only in his imagination. My right hon. friend was wrong every time he stated that taxation in Canada is higher than in Great Britain and the other British Dominions. Canada has the lowest taxation of them all.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I was expecting my right hon. friend to say No, and I have come with some ammunition. The first thing I did was to inquire as to the income tax and I have here an official communication from the Commissioner of Taxation, comparing the income tax in Canada with that paid in Great Britain and the other British Dominions. This is a very interesting statement:

I will not ask the House to bear with me while I give the taxation on every income. Let me only say that the taxation continues in the same proportion until you reach incomes of between $150,000 and $200,000. On an income of $200,000 the Canadian pays $97,849.50, while in Great Britain the taxation amounts to $94,948.67. The same proportion continues until you reach an income of $1,000,000, but my right hon. friend will agree with me that the number of Canadians who pay taxes on an income of that size is rather microscopic and that the bulk of the Canadian people is less heavily taxed than the people of Great Britain and the other British Dominions so far as income tax is concerned.
What about municipal taxation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Let us come to that. I asked the Bureau of Statistics about it and here is the answer I received:
The taxation revenue per head of population in the United Kingdom is $79.37.
The taxation revenue per head of population in Australia is $43.09.
The taxation revenue per head of population in New Zealand is $60.97.
The taxation revenue per head of population in Canada is $36.67.
If my hon. friend will permit me, he does not mean to suggest that is the taxation revenue, he means the income tax revenue?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Oh no, I will give the
details if it suits my hon. friend.
Does that include provincial taxation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It does so far as Australia is concerned, it does not in the case of the other countries which are not administered in the same way. But the proposition is so vastly different that we have no hesitation at all-and any expert in taxation I have spoken to agrees in saying that Canada is the lowest-taxed country in the British Empire.

Have you the figures with
respect to the United States in that statement of taxation revenue?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, I have just read
in the Congressional Record of the United States a speech by a gentleman whose name I cannot remember, the chairman of the Appropriations committee, and his statement is that the United States is the most heavily taxed country in the world. I agree with my hon. friend that the income taxation there is less than in Canada, but they have all sorts of other taxes which weigh heavily on the shoulders of their population, and any American will tell you so.

My hon. friend did not
ascertain the figures from the Bureau of Statistics.
Mr. LAPOINTE. I did not. My reason for not doing so is that my conflict with the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) has reference to the financial position of the British Dominions and not the United States.

I understood my hon.
friend to say that the taxation revenue for Canada was $36 per capita?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

I am quite sure that the impression my hon. friend is giving is wholly wrong; it may not be intentional on his part, I am sure it is not. The per capita taxation of Canada is somewhere around $250 per head.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, that is the debt per capita, not the taxation. I have in my hand a statement by Sir Henry Gibson, chairman of the Parliamentary committee of the National Union of Manufacturers in Great Britain. I took it from the December number

The Address-Mr. Lapointe
of the English Review. I quote it in part:
Since the recent great war, owing to the fact that we have balanced our budget and are paying off our debt, our taxation is much higher than that of any other country in the world, thus increasing the cost of home manufactures.
There is no doubt as to that, and we must admire Britain in that respect. Whatever else can be said of Britain it must be conceded that she deals earnestly with serious problems. Britain financed her Allies during the war. She did not repudiate any debt. She did not leave the payment of those debts to posterity. She has taxed her people heavily, she is meeting her obligations, and she is giving to the world an example of honest international dealings. All honour to Great Britain for that! But, Mr. Speaker, we could not do the same in Canada, probably on account of our proximity to the United States.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My right hon. friend says " hear, hear," and he is right. But why complain of our heavy taxation when other nations, and other peoples, are a good deal more heavily taxed than we are?
4 p.m. A gentleman was saying the other day, an acquaintance of my right hon. friend, that our income taxation in this country was a confiscation of capital. He was wrong, and I have shown he was wrong. Moreover if you decrease the income tax, when it has been decreased with the present financial condition of the country, somebody else will have to pay. That gentleman would like to confiscate the comforts of life which poorer people have, but which they could not have if the price of the commodities they use was increased.
My right hon. friend referred many times to the French treaty. On all platforms from which he spoke in the country he did so. He also referred to the subject when the leader of the government was speaking the other day. Of course, in his opinion that treaty is no good; it never had any merit. It pleases my right hon. friend to throw ridicule on the French treaty. He said the other day that apart from wheat our exports to France had decreased.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Well, Hansard will show. My right hon. friend is suffering from loss of memory.

I rarely suffer from that. What I said was this-that the whole in-

crease, and more than the increase, was made up by wheat and other goods not affected by the treaty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think my right hon. friend is wrong even in that contention.
That is what I was told by a government officer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There are many articles in which there was a heavy increase. My hon. friend for Brantford (Mr. Raymond) referred yesterday to the subject of agricultural implements. Since the treaty came into force we have exported $1,431,428 of agricultural implements. That is since September last. During the same period of last year we exported $796,842 worth. There has been an increase of 100 per cent in agricultural implements alone. And let me say en passant that I am pleased to see that the manufacturers of implements can compete with the world on a foreign market. There has also been an increase in various articles, mainly parts of automobiles, electrical apparatus, and aluminum ware. I have a further authority which my right hon. friend will not dispute. In July last the annual convention of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association was held in Toronto. Attached to that body is a tariff committee which presented a report. That report appeared in the July issue of Industrial Canada and here is what I read:
The Convention-
Meaning the treaty.
-removes all discriminations against Canada in favour of the United States, and in addition provides for substantial tariff preference on a considerable list of the products of each country.
And that report was carried unanimously. Surely the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) will remove from his mind this idea of brandy and wine with regard to the French treaty and admit that we did some good and that the manufacturers of the country have received it' with commendation.
Would the hon. gentleman give us some returns in respect to lobsters and salmon?
And condensed milk?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
put that question on the order paper, I shall be glad. I cannot carry that information about with me.
There is another treaty which has received the sarcastic criticism of my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen). I refer to the famous Hali-

The Address-Mr. Lapointe
but treaty. My right hon. friend has paraded the Halibut treaty from the Atlantic to the Pacific for the last six months. He has charged me with having "elbowed aside" the British Ambassador at Washington for the purpose of affixing my signature to that treaty, and he has repeated periodically that, as a result, the treaty is not valid; that the United States Senate has refused it, and that there is no Halibut treaty. My right hon. friend knows that that statement is not according to the facts. Last year, when the treaty was under discussion in this House, he admitted that the signature had nothing to do with the attitude of the Senate.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My right hon. friend
admitted it.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Will my right hon.
friend permit me, to-morrow, to quote what
he said on that occasion?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Thank you, I will.
Another instance of loss of memory 1 Let me tell my right hon. friend that the signature on the treaty had nothing to do with the rider which was attached by the Senate afterwards. The Canadian government took the stand that, as this was a purely Canadian affair concerning only Canada and the United States, the treaty should be negotiated and signed by a Canadian minister, and it was so signed. Unfortunately, this was at the end of a session of the United States congress. The treaty was submitted to the Senate of the United States m the dying hours of the session, and that riuer, which had nothing to do with the signature, which was for the purpose of changing the wording of the treaty, wording which had been prepared and suggested by the Americans themselves, was not called to the attention of the authorities of the United States. I may tell my right hon. friend that he is mistaken in his prediction. I have the strongest assurance on the strongest authority that the Senate of the United States will not insist on that rider, and that the treaty will be ratified at the present session of Congress.

The statement which I
made and which the hon. member contradicted was that there was no Halibut treaty. Does he say again that there is a Halibut treaty?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is a treaty which waits for the ratification of the American Senate, and I have every confidence that it will be ratified.
There may be, some day.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This prediction of my
right hon. friend is no more founded than is his prediction about the result of the next election. When my right hon. friend ventures predictions on the next election, in order to be taken seriously, he says as he did in Toronto the other day:	"Gentlemen, the
next government will be the most unpopular in the history of Canada." It will have to go a long way to beat the record of the National Liberal and Conservative government.
Another statement of facts which I desire to correct, since I was a party to the controversy, is with regard to the cancellation of a contract which was granted to Canadian-Vickers after the election of 1921 for the construction of an ice-breaker for an amount of $1,580,000. My hon. friend said the other day that the amount was about one milliion dollars. It is $1,580,000, and the Mikula which has been purchased by the government has cost, laid down at Quebec in first class repair, a total of $437,115.73. This includes all the repairs which were made after a certificate of Lloyds had been secured. The vessel was delivered to Canada as good as new, and the country has saved over one million dollars, my hon. friend nothwithstanding.
There is another fact which was criticized while my right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) was speaking. This is in connection with the famous dry-dock at Victoria. My leader was told that that dry-dock had been started in 1911. Of course, it had nothing to do with the elections! These are the facts. In 1911, an application had been made by a private company, under the name of the Esquimalt Dry-dock and Shipbuilding Company, for the usual subsidy granted for the construction of a dry-dock; but this was abandoned and nothing was done until 1914. Then the government purchased land for constructing a dry-dock at Esquimalt at a cost of $346,221.25. Curiously enough, however, it was demonstrated that this land was not suitable as a site for a dry-dock. It is still there unused; I saw it there last fall. But it was only on the 24th December, 1919, a month or so after the election of my good friend, the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie) that an order in council was passed granting authority to expropriate a new site called Skinner's Cove. This new site has cost the country $54,388.03. When this government came into office, a sum of over $1,000,000

The Address

Mr. Lapointe

had already been expended, and, of course, the construction of the dry-dock had to be continued. I am afraid that is not the only expenditure at Victoria which has left on the country a crushing load. I have in my hand a document concerning the construction of four wooden ships at Victoria. Under an order in council, passed during that same month of December, 1919, Canada agreed to furnish for each vessel a sum of $175,000, the builders having to contribute a sum of $75,000. The country was to have a first mortgage on the vessels, bearing interest at the rate of 6 per cent per annum. I will not, however, discuss this matter except to give the result and to show when there was such extravagance in the administration of the affairs of the country as is described in certain newspapers. The country	has paid	$644,050.65 for
the construction of those four wooden ships. Only one of them has been completed, and it had to be completed by the government itself, the material being sold afterwards. The whole revenue to the government amounts to $32.-
063..60 out of $600,000. The boat was sold for $22,000, the materials for $9,000, and sundries $1,063.60. What is queer about the whole transaction is that my predecessor in the Department of Marine was strongly opposed to the giving of that money for the construction of wooden ships at Victoria. I have a letter written by him to my hon. friend, the then Minister of Finance, and also a letter from him to the Right Hon. Sir George E. Foster, prior to the passing of that order in council. Later on-and this is still more conspicuously strange -I find a letter from him dated April, 1920, which reads:
Dear Dr. Toi.mte,
I have given the matter further consideration regarding the Marine Department's supervising the construction of brigantine sailing ships that are being built largely at public expense at Victoria. You are aware that I was very much opposed to this proposition from the start, and, while I would like very much to oblige you, I really cannot have anything to do with it myself nor allow my department to be connected with it in any way.
Yours faithfully,
C. C. Ballantynb.
What does this mean? It means that that government gave $600,000 of the money of the country to a company for the construction of four wooden ships with which the Minister of Marine refused to have anything to do, and refused to allow the supervision of the work in a proper way, and the result is that the country has lost practically all the money that was given. This is an example of the administration which we had prior to December, 1921.
(Mr. Lapointe.]
Now, my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) when he was in the city of Quebec delivered an address to the citizens; and after having made many statements to which I have referred, he paid me a compliment,-well, I do not know whether the compliment was to me or to himself. He said that his imperialism and Ernest Lapointe's imperialism were the same.
I never said that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The newspapers said it, then.
Forgive me for that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The world changes, and
people change with the world. We see the truth of this to-day in the Old Country where people who were branded as disloyal and who were given a very bad reputation not very long ago are now ministers of the Crown in Great Britain. And there is a considerable change in this country. After what was said about myself and those who thought as I did not so long ago, it seems now that there i3 no difference between my right hon. friend and me. Well the right hon. gentleman should not charge me with elbowing British ambassadors here and there; that is somewhat different. There was a difference also last year. The House will recall that famous telegram which was sent to the British dominions by the former government of Great Britain when a crisis, or what seemed to some people a crisis, threatened in the Near East. This government took the attitude, I think very properly, that we required an explanation and detailed information before sending any answer. We were criticized for that by my right hon. friend. In Toronto he said that the duty of the government should have been to reply, as he himself said, "Ready, aye ready." My right hon. friend nods his head in assent. Perhaps it might interest him to hear what the late Mr. Bonar Law had to say about this matter.

What I said in Toronto
I said in Quebec. The hon. member has quoted only one small disconnected part of my statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My right hon. friend went to Toronto to deliver his famous " Ready, aye ready " declaration, and that is why I mentioned Toronto. Here is what the late Right Hon. Mr. Bonar Law said only a few weeks, I should say a few days, after that message had been despatched:
To throw suddenly, as a bolt from the blue, this appeal for help when not one of the dominions had the remotest idea that there was any need of it, and when it was well known that their help could not come in

The Address-^Mr. Lapointe
time to be of any assistance in the crisis, was to risk, in my opinion, one of the greatest assets of this Empire.
It was to take a risk with our dominions which no wise man would have taken and which I think was not more foolish than it was wrong.
That appeal, characterized by Mr. Bonar
Law as being both foolish and wrong, my right hon. friend would have received with the assurance " Ready, aye ready." I do not hesitate to say that my right hon. friend is not a safe leader when there are war clouds still hanging over nations.
May I say, while on this subject, a word or two about the recent Imperial Conference.
I desire to congratulate my right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his associates on the work they accomplished there. The Prime Minister acted as a true British statesman, jealous of the rights and the autonomy of his own country, but just as keen an exponent of the rights of the other units of the Empire. 1 was sorry that my right hon. friend tried to throw some ridicule on the position of my leader at the Imperial Conference. That is not dignified political warfare. The task of my right hon. leader was appreciated differently by those who witnessed his work there, and by an almost, I might say entirely, unanimous British press. I am glad that this last conference vindicated the idea that led to these gatherings, namely, that they are conferences merely and by no means an executive committee. These gatherings are intended to allow various British prime ministers to meet together and confer, exchanging views and communicating opinions, wishing one another well, trying to help one another, but preserving all the time each his own personal individuality.	And it should be so; any
attempt to transform these conferences into a body with more power would be a step towards destruction.
In view of certain statements which were made by one or two of the delegates to the last conference after the result of the recent British elections, I think it is well that we should express our own views in the matter. They are mistaken who believe that the decision of any such conference is binding, either upon the dominions or upon Great Britain herself The parliament of Canada will never subscribe to this doctrine, and it does not expect th^ parliament of Great Britain to subscribe to it either. Those decisions are not any more binding when they relate to fiscal matters or imperial preference than when they relate to naval or other policies. It is preposterous to think that the people of Great Britain could be bound to a policy which they might have rejected 21i
at the polls by an overwhelming vote. Canadians would resent any contention that an imperial conference might interfere with our mode of raising revenue; and surely we must admit that the people of Great Britain have the same right. May I say also that we are quite able to speak for ourselves in this part of the world, and that I deny the right of any British statesman who comes to this country to go back to Great Britain and presume to represent the feelings of Canada? For instance, I have seen reports of speeches in Great Britain and editorials in British papers describing the sorrow that was manifested everywhere in Canada at the result of the last British elections. I have never seen such sorrow in this country. We are giving Great Britain a preference in our market of our own free will and because it suits us; and, Mr. Speaker, we must not forget that our goods are admitted free into Great Britain while British goods are paying duty in this country. To state that Great Britain does not act fairly w.th us by refusing to tax the goods of other countries while admitting our own free is sheer nonsense. Certain gentlemen-and they were the leaders of the tariff preference campaign in Great Britain-advocated free trade within the Empire. Now, whatever may be the merits of this policy-and I do not want to give my own opinion on it to-day-I may call to the notice of our manufacturers that they are already objecting, many of them strongly, to the volume of British goods now coming into this country undei the preferential tariff. I ask them what wornd the importations be if we had free trade? All this shows that fiscal autonomy is just as necessary to this country as political autonomy, and that every nation within the Empire must be left free to devise its own fiscal policies according to its needs and the wishes of its people.
My hon. friend from Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) complained that a subject was mentioned in the Speech from the Throne but there was no declaration of policy in regard to it. I refer to the St. Lawrence waterway scheme. Well, there are strong supporters and advocates of this great project, and there are equally strong objectors. Is it not, then, the part of wisdom to see that all the scientific and engineering investigation necessary is made before we commit ourselves to the execution of the project? Even the report of the International Joint Waterways Commission suggested that a further investigation should be made by an enlarged engineering board. Now, to those who are

The Address-'Mr. Lapointe
very strongly opposed to this project let me say this: First, no scheme will be entered into at any time as far as I am concerned-and I think it is the policy of the government- until it is clearly shown that the present level of the St. Lawrence river at all points will never be lowered as a result of the works to be carried out; second, that all rights which any of the provinces may possess will be properly safeguarded. It has been stated in the course of this debate that there is strong opposition to the scheme in some parts of the province of Quebec. I admit there is. Per. haps there are misapprehensions which may be cleared up as the result of the investigations to be made. But let me say in this connection that the former government made a mistake, indeed a blunder, when it deprived Quebec of its representation on the International Joint Waterways Board and replaced Mr. Justice Mignault by a gentleman who had been rejected at the polls by the electors of Ontario. Quebec was and is supremely interested in this scheme. I think every hon. member will agree with me that it was a blunder to take away from the board the only representative of the province of Quebec and not replace him by another representative from that province, because the report of such a board, upon which Quebec had no representation, although it is so supremely interested, could not carry with the citizens of the province the weight of confidence which would otherwise have been the case.
My right hon. friend referred to a certain election which took place in the county of Kent, and the part which I am supposed to have taken in that election. My right hon. friend spoke of the terrible bribing policy carried on by the government in that county, and he said I went in a repentant mood and told the. electors that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police would not go there any more for the enforcement of the fisheries laws. Is that a crime of ,first magnitude? When I went down to the county I met my genial friend the member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) in the city of Moncton, and the first thing I did was to buy a copy of that good Conservative newspaper, the Daily Times, which I found contained a report of a speech delivered the preceding day by my hon. friend himself. Here is what I read:
It was by Mr. Lapointe's department that the Royal Northwest Mounted Police had been sent into the county of Kent. Never before in history had the armed forces of Canada been used for the enforcement of legislation regarding fisheries or any other regulations. They were only used in criminal matters and in cases where the civil authorities were unable to deal with the situation.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My right hon. friend
says, "hear, hear," so he made the statement; I am glad to know it. In the same newspaper I read the following editorial comment-I shall quote only part of it:
Mr. Lapointe treated the fishermen as outlaws; never before in the history of this province were an honest and hard-toiling body of men subjected to such vexatious, aggravating and ill-advised treatment.
When I was accused of being such a tyrant I investigated the matter and I found that it had been the policy of the Department of Marine and Fisheries since 1920 to use the mounted police for the enforcement of fisheries regulations. That policy was originated by the former government, and I found in the records of the department after the election that one of those who asked for that so-called reform was a leading member of the Conservative party-I think he was its chief organizer in Kent during the recent election campaign. My own opinion is that fisheries regulations can be enforced without the use of soldiers or the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and I was pleased to declare that as long as I was Minister of Marine and Fisheries no more mounted police should go into Kent county. I hope that my hon. friend who is now administering the department (Mr. Cardin) will carry on with the promise I made -not a promise, but a statement, and I abide by it. Was there anything wrong in that? Having been charged by the gentlemen who were responsible for that change in the enforcement of the regulations with having committed such a crime, was there anything wrong in saying to them, "I am confident myself that the police are not needed in the enforcement of fisheries regulations, and that they should not be used for that purpose; if the Department of Marine needs such officers or supervisors they should appoint them from the civil population of Canada?"
May I ask the hon. gentleman how it happens that it took him two and a half years to find that that was the policy of this department,-that he never found that out until the eve of the Kent election?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend's arithmetic is as wrong as his statement-with regard to the two and a half years. My hon. friends were in office when that policy was inaugurated.
Now, about those elections in Halifax and Kent, my right hon. friend took the attitude the other day of a triumphant, victorious general. Well I do not see that there

The Address-[DOT]Mr. Lapointe
is anything in the result for my right hon. friend to write home about. He was not there; he went to the county of Cape Breton North and Victoria. I am told that prior to his visit there we were not too sure of the election, but it came out all right afterwards. Kent and Halifax were carried without my right hon. friend, and his friends from there should have wired him on the night of the election in the terms of that historic phrase, "Brave Crillon, pends-toi, nous avons vaincu sans toil"
Translate it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, I am afraid I cannot translate it-"Brave Crillon, hang yourself; we have conquered without you!" But that election was characterized by appeals which do no credit to any of the gentlemen who indulged in them, because they were sectional appeals and appeals to national discussion. Now, I have the newspapers with me; that is the safe way when you make statements with regard to what the newspapers have said. The government was represented as having sold the East to the West, more particularly in the Crows-nest pass agreement. It is remarkable the number of times the country is for sale. We are supposed to have sold the East last year and we are told to-day that we are still selling it to the western farmers. My hon. friend from Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion), suggested a reciprocity in that sort of trade when he said that our western friends were selling their birthright for a mess of pottage; so there is sale on both sides.
I said Esau sold his.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; so it is an extraordinary fact that that mercantile wickedness is prevailing everywhere. Well, while these hon. gentlemen were saying in Kent and Halifax that the East was being sold to the West, my right hon. friend, as the newspapers of the time will show, was in Saskatoon and Edmonton singing a love duet with Hon. Robert Rogers on a platform of reconciliation, and both were saying that the government had betrayed the interests of the West, had violated their pledges to the western farmers, and were not carrying out [DOT]any of the promises made to them. Tory tactics, Tory methods-
Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am glad my right
hon. friend stands up when I say that.
Oh, oh.

I enjoy the wit of the
hon. gentleman as much as his friends do; it is his great asset. What I wanted to say was merely this: I stated as regards betrayal at Edmonton and Saskatoon exactly what I have stated in this House and no more, and I stated in western Canada what I stated in eastern Canada with respect to the Crows-nest pass.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If my right hon. friend
is satisfied with what he has just said, he does not in the least contradict my statement. It does not matter whether he said it in the House as well as in the West; I am merely concerned with what he said in the West. As I was saying when my right hon. friend stood up, that is Tory tactics, Tory methods, Tory duplicity, Tory appeals to division in this country.
Read it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Every one of us feels proud of the part of the country in which he lives and which is dear to him. But, Sir, if Canada is to be a great country, Maritime province rights, western rights, central Canada rights, must be subordinate to the national duty of all Canadians to build up a country undivided and indivisible, the home of a big, united people. To the accomplishment of that task we will endeavour to devote all our energies. It is my earnest hope that there will always be in this country a big party which will be the supreme line _ of defence, protecting Canada against division and disruption, by trying to meet in a reasonable way the views of Canadians in all sections of the country, and by trying to satisfy so far as is possible what they represent to us as their needs. No Canadian, whether he lives in the West or in the East, should concentrate his vision and mould his opinion as if Canada ended at lake Superior. There are advantages and obstacles in this country, but I hope the former outweigh the latter; indeed, that they are predominant. Of course, they are caused by geographical and economic conditions, and what we should try and do is always to consider the interests of the nation as a whole, and not the interests of an individual or of any set of individuals. We should try, not to build up a city or a district, but to build up a great Canadian nation. If to accomplish that we have to resort to some compromise, if we have to follow some middle course, I contend and believe that that course is a national duty. Any man who tries to align agriculture against industry in this country
31'G

The Address-'Mr. Lapointe
or industry against agriculture is not doing his duty to this country.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am glad I have struck a responsive chord in the heart of my hon. friend.
I wish you would make a start and keep on in the right direction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am going to keep on that way to the end of my remarks.
Be consistent that long.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We are proud of the progress of industry in this country. It has progressed by leaps and bounds, and I am glad of it. It deserves all encouragement. But we must not forget that agriculture is the basis of our national life. I had the privilege of visiting the western provinces in the course of recent months. If that is a crime, I plead guilty, and I intend to commit it again. I have seen the wonderful crops in Saskatchewan and Alberta, and whatever opinion we may have of the views of the western farmer there is one thing of which we may all be proud, and that is that they produce more food per capita in the western provinces than anywhere else in the world. One cannot but regret that they are not receiving for their work and their investment better returns. Doubtless the conditions prevailing throughout the world are largely responsible for that, and I hope those conditions will remedy themselves in the course of time.
I have not much respect for those who answer the farmers or the grain growers when they submit their grievances, that they should change their method of farming. I do not think our manufacturing friends would be satisfied, when they themselves submit the conditions which affect them, if they were answered: Well, devote your time and your energy to some other industry, produce something else.
I do not think my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) was altogether fair yesterday when he suggested to the farmers of the West that the home market was their salvation, and that they should wait until that market is increased. Whatever may be the merits or the demerits of the proposal I am sure that our friends from the West desire to have their remedy in the course of their lifetime at least, if not in this generation, and they did not seem to be inclined to follow my hon. friend into

his kingdom of Utopia. I believe that what is needed is that every one in this country whether he lives in the East or the West, whether he grows wheat or works in an industrial concern, should feel that he is receiving from the government of this country an equal measure of justice; I think that everybody will agree with me in that statement. The sense of grievance in the heart or mind of any Canadian is harmful and cannot but work injury. Recriminations and denunciations are of no avail. Nothing can be built on them.
What is imperatively needed in this country is to knit afresh national brotherhood. A great Italian statesman, Mazzini, used to say that young Italy was the polar star of his thoughts. Let a united Canada be the polar star of all our actions, of all our policies. Let it be our one supreme ambition, and let every Canadian devote his time and his energy to accomplishing that end, and to building up a great and prosperous nation.
Mr. ALEXANDRE J. DOUCET (Kent, A ,B.):	Mr.	Speaker, may I have the
temerity to follow such an eloquent speaker as the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe)? I wish at the outset, Mr. Speaker, to congratulate you upon the honourable position which you occupy in this chamber. Representing as you do a county whose population is largely of French-Acadian descent, and knowing that you are familiar with their customs, the hardships they have had to endure in years long past, and the lack of educational facilities they have had to contend with, I trust that if in this debate, I infringe upon the rules or the procedure of this House you will readily understand that it will be through lack of knowledge, and not through wish or intent. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that I had intended to open my remarks in the French language, the language which I cherish, the language which I learnt at my mother's knee, the language of five-sixths of the population of my constituency, but I do not wish to delay this debate and I intend to use the language of the majority, one of the two great languages of this country, and one of the two official languages of this House.
We are told in the Speech from the Throne that:
National unity, not less than national prosperity, depends upon the surmounting of those barriers which have tended to separate western from eastern Canada, and to discourage permanent settlement upon the land.
Those, Mr. Speaker, are very nice words, but so far as some of the representatives on the other side of the House are concerned,

The
Address-Mr. Doucet
they are really vain words. If you will read the speeches made during this debate by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. d'Anjou) and the hon. member for Vaudreuil-Soulanges (Mr. Ouimet) you will recognize immediately that these hon. gentlemen are not striving for national unity. What they are seeking to do is to perpetuate the disunion which has prevailed for a number of years past, largely owing to political machinations unworthy of men occupying seats in this Chamber.
Mr. Speaker, I belong to the French-Acadian race who established and colonized in 1605 the first village of white people on this northern hemisphere. Our clergy through the Jesuit fathers, were also the first to enunciate pleas in behalf of civilization and Christianity in 1611. From the sturdy population of those pioneer days sprang men such as Mr. Amand Landry who when called upon to sacrifice his principles in 1857, spoke as follows in the legislative assembly at Frederiction-and I may explain that he was the father of Sir. Pierre A. Landry, who occupied a seat in this House and was afterwards elevated to the bench of New Brunswick:
My forefathers preferred the spoliation of their property and exile rather than taking the oath of allegiance which they held in abhorrence. I would be unworthy of them if I should accept this money to betray my political party. I would be dishonoured by such an action. I want to hand down to my children and to my fellow countnunen a name unblemished and revered. I very strongly decline your offer. Give back that money to those who have sent you to me, and tell them that although the Frenchman, as I am called here, may be poor, there is not enough gold in the world to corrupt him.
Sir, I am pleased indeed to follow the principles of the great Liberal-Conservative party laid down by such men as the late Sir. John A. Macdonald and Sir George Etienne Cartier as the principles upon which this great Dominion could be built up and best fulfil its destiny.
Is it true that my hon. friend ran as a farmer candidate in New Brunswick in 1921?
It is not true.

Being a new member, Mr. Speaker, I would crave the indulgence -of hon. members opposite. I am not averse to crossexamination but I should like to say this-if my hon. friends will only be patient and wait a little while they will lose nothing by it. As to my position and candidature in 1921 I shall make that plain when the proper time comes. I wish to say that, while I belong to the French-Acadian race and profess the same creed as the hon. members for Rimouski and Vaudreuil-Soulanges, I follow proudly, as
I have already said, the principles laid down by Macdonald and Cartier. It was the latter,
I believe, who said that the last gun fired in the Dominion for the defence of British institutions would be fired by a French-Canadian. Let me say that the first gun to be fired-and God forbid that the day should ever come when such action will be necessary-in defence of the French language and the Catholic faith in this Dominion will be fired by a French Acadian.
We have heard something of by-elections in this country, and the last speaker referred to the by-election in Kent county, New Brunswick. Of course all hon. members know there was an election in that county.

Tlie Minister of Justice
knows it.

Yes, he undoubtedly does. The Prime Minister when he spoke in this debate said there had been thirty-four byelections .-ince the government had succeeded to office and that the government had only lost two. That is not a great deviation from the truth, and yet when you closely analyse exactly what happened during the last two years you will find that out'of the thirty-four by-elections, twenty have reference to gentlemen appointed tc offices of emolument who went back to their constituents for reelection. It would be unnatural to suppose, under the circums'ances that those men should not secure re-election, especially when we remember that their constituencies in 1920 and 1921 had voted Liberal by majorities running all the way from 2,000 to 7,000. Since that time there have been several by-elections, including one to which the Minister of Justice referred, Cape Breton North and Victoria. The minister said the right hon. leader of the opposition had been in that county. He did visit the constituency, but, whatever the result of the election is at-5 p.m. tributable to, the Liberal majority of 3,339 in 1921 was cut down to a minority in the recent contest. The hon. gentleman \Mr. Kelly) who now sits for that constituency does not represent p. majority of the voters in the riding. There was also a by-election in North Essex when the Liberal majority of 7,195 was cut down to 1,027. No, it would not have

The county is plastered with Liberal orators, submerged in Liberal rum, and polluted with Liberal money. They are scared blue and they are resorting to all the tactics known to civilization, heathenism, idolatry and low-down "Injun" cunning in order to

Mr. Speaker, while to a
certain degree I am annoyed, I am not surprised at the attitude taken by hon. gentlemen opposite, because I am free to admit that the Kent county by-election must have been such a fatal blow to their hopes that they can only regard it as the sinister forerunner of what is to happen to the Liberal party when it next appeals to the country.
Before laying before the House the issues upon which we conducted the campaign in Kent county, I have a few precious gems, selected from campaign speeches made by the right hon. leader of the government (Mr. Mackenzie King), the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Copp) and the hon. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) in the election of 1921. First I quote from The Transcript- certainly an organ which was not prejudiced against my friend the Secretary of State-its report of a speech made by him at that time in these words:	[DOT]
He pronounced his policy in regard to the railway situation as to be strongly in favour of retaining the I.C.R. at its old status.
The electors of Kent county were asked by the Secretary of State and others' to support the Liberal administration because they had fulfilled their promises. Have they fulfilled their promise in connection with the Intercolonial railway, when it is true that the Hanna board in 1921 had given a public

The Address-Mr. Doucet
decision that they would include in the Atlantic region the Intercolonial, the Transcontinental and all branches east of Montreal, including the Grand Trunk line to Portland? They took charge of the administration of affairs, and the Intercolonial railway was cut off at Riviere du Loup, and the Transcontinental at Monk, so the eastern section of the railway system is about one-tenth of the whole mileage.
In The Transcript of October 14, 1921, the Secretary of State is reported as follows:
Mr. Copp expressed his policy as being to take the I.C.R. out of the hands of the Toronto people who are using it for their own gain, and hand it back to the people of the Maritime provinces for whom it was built; and, furthermore, to bring back the many people who were forced to leave their homes here and go to Toronto.
You would imagine, Mr. Speaker, from the declarations on the other side condemning the stirring up of sectional prejudice that our hon. friend would never have been guilty of making such an appeal. He did, however, in 1921, in spite of the fact that Mr. D. B. Hanna at that time said:
There had not been one man taken from Moncton, but that because of his competency he had been promoted to a larger sphere; and the same thing was happening in Winnipeg. In the management of a large system there had to be a consolidation of accounts, and everyone knows there has to be a central place where the accounts can be gathered. Not one man on the board of directors wished or desired to disturb anyone, but the exigencies of the situation compelled such an action.
Now, at that time Mr. Hanna explained to the country, and to those who had been more or less opposed to him because of the fact that men had been removed from Moncton to Toronto, that in each and every case promotion had taken place. In the spring of 1923 a large number of men were removed from the constituency represented by the Secretary of State and _ were transferred to the city of Montreal. I have no fault to find with any administration of the railways that would transfer men for the purpose of bettering the efficiency of the system; but I do complain that men who in 1923 were transferred from the offices in Moncton to Montreal, and were receiving $135 per month, were, within a few weeks later, forced to see their salaries diminished to $98 per month. I have yet to hear any public pronouncement from the Secretary of State in disapproval of such reductions. May I be permitted to refer to some of the issues that were raised in Kent? I defy any member on the opposite side to quote anything to show that I personally- and Sir, I can only speak for myself, because I carried on the campaign alone-

Where was the hon.
member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson)?

When the hon. member
for York-Sunbury spoke, I did not accompany him, therefore I did not hear what he said. If he said anything that my hon. friends opposite object to, he will have a chance to express his opinion on that in the House. I wish hon. members to take note of the reasons why public sentiment in the county of Kent expressed itself on the 20th of December last in opposition to the present administration. In doing this I believe I am rendering a service to my county, and at the same time, if they are wise enough to give heed to it, I may be rendering a service also to the present government.
We had in mind the subject of immigration. in the first place, and regret was expressed at the extent of the exodus of our people to the country to the south of us. We spoke of increased taxation, of increased remuneration to men in high places, and of the policy announced at that time, and since put into effect, of reducing the expenditure on the civil service by turning out in the cold men in the lower positions while retaining at high salaries those in the upper places. We spoke also of the royal commissions, seven of which, I believe, were operating at that time. I need not dwell very long upon that; hon. members must have seen some of their reports. I venture to say, however, that the majority of these reports will not be read by anyone but by the man who is paid to read them. As a well-known eastern paper said, the whole sum and substance of these reports would be worth much less than thirty cents.
We dealt also with the question of railway rates; there is some dissatisfaction in connection with the present state of affairs in matters of transportation. We also made reference to the lack of markets; to the sending of Canadian goods through Canadian ports; and, last but not least, to the development of interprovincial trade. I should like, in the limited time available, to discuss these various questions, but I have , not an opportunity of doing so now, I may have occasion later in the session, to place my position on these matters fairly before the House.
I have told you, Mr. Speaker, of the great number of men bearing gifts who were in Kent county during the by-election campaign, but notwithstanding all these offers of gifts, the county could not be bought. I have here another gem which I think I should read to the
