House, dealing with the necessity to beware of
the man bringing gifts. It reads:
The good and kindly Veniot With his promises so calming To save his Liberal party From a premature embalming.
Oh, Mr. Copp, Oh, Mr. Copp,
The railway will extend,
Judicially he ever is Copp's and the people's friend.
It's sad and sorry work,
To keep the ship afloat.
But Copp will get no judgeship If Doucette "Copps" the vote.
Arthur comes in hot haste At the voice of King, his master,
To prevent a repetition Of that Halifax Disaster.
If these big guns be air guns To avert impending wreck,
They bring a long range cannon To belch from Old Quebec.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, the electors of Kent county were afraid of men bearing gifts. As the Trojans said of old, "Timeo Danaos et dona ferentes,"-I fear the Liberals even bringing gifts.
May I make some reference to the rewards given to those who took part in the Kent county campaign? In this instance, as you must know, failure rather than merit was being rewarded. First, we have the hon. Minister of Marine (Mr. Lapointe), promoted to the position of Minister of Justice. Then we have the hon. member for Richelieu (Mr. Cardin) promoted to the position of Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I want to say frankly, that as there had to be a Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and as, so far, the present party has to remain in power,
I am glad to see my hon. friend in a ministerial seat. Even though he was not successful, he certainly deserves a reward for the great amount of energy he displayed in that campaign. Then we have a third man who took part in the campaign, Mr. Arthur T. Leblanc, of Campbellton. He was appointed a judge of the Supreme Court of New Brunswick.
Does my hon. friend mean that Mr. Leblanc is not qualified for the position of Judge of the Supreme Court, or that he was disqualified because he went into Kent county?
I did not say anything of the kind, but I will say that he was as well qualified as any other prospective candidate for the judgeship.	[DOT]
The hon. gentleman to your immediate right did not think so.

The hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) can speak for
	u
himself, and it is not necessary-that I should take up the time of the House in answering for the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson). There are others who took part in the Kent county by-election campaign who have not yet been rewarded. In this connection I wish to remind the House that the hon. member for Restigouche and Madawaska (Mr. Michaud) has not been rewarded. Why? Was it because he was the only one of the whole delegation who talked politics and did not raise the racial issue? I submit to my genial friend that his reward is due, and it is the vacant senatorship for the province of New Brunswick. There are two other gentlemen, one from Kincardine, Ontario, and the other from Fredericton, N.B. who also need rewards, and on their behalf I would suggest that the leader of the government ask his cabinet to create a new royal commission entitled "How did it happen in Kent?"
In order to reward all those who took part, Mr. Speaker, and there were twenty-two, I believe, you would have to create a new royal commission, and that would be for the purpose of creating national unity between the two great races of this Dominion, and to that commission I would suggest that Mr. Theriault, local member for the county of L'lslet, the member for Rimouski and the member for Vaudreuil-Soulanges be appointed. They would possibly be able to determine what is requisite, and the proper means to adopt, in order to bring about national unity in this country. Their utterances are testimony to that.
An hon. member of this House asked me a moment ago if I had forgotten that I was a Farmer's candidate in 1921. In 1921 the humble member for Kent was not a Farmer's candidate; he was not a Progressive candidate. In order to show where I stood on that occasion I am going to weary the House by placing on Hansard for the edification of those who seem to glory in the fact that possibly the member for Kent was a Progressive candidate, in 1921, my platform. It is as follows:
(1)	We believe in friendly relations and the teaching of mutual respect between the two great races which compose this Dominion.
(2)	In the matter of tariff, we favor protection for our industries, in order to give our farmers, fishermen and lumbermen a home market.
(3)	We believe that the farming and labour elements of this country are not sufficiently represented in the different governments of our Dominion, and that better consideration should be given to the agricultural and industrial problems of the country.
(4)	We regret that our federal ministers of late years have not been sufficiently in touch with the different sections of the country, particularly the Maritime provinces, and we assert that this is the only way to obtain responsible government.

The Address-Mr. Doucet
(5)	We believe that the Department of Trade and Commerce should get into more intimate contact with the public in the way of pointing out and assisting in finding markets for the people.
(6)	We maintain that our representatives in Parliament should be free to support, without detriment to Canada, the party which would consider and solve the various Maritime provinces' problems, such as transportation, markets, unemployment, and the greater developments of our national resources and possibilities and in this respect we advocate:
(a)	The establishment of abattoirs and cold storage systems at central points in the Maritime provinces.
(b)	The establishment of an experimental farm in one of the north shore counties, with equal facilities for the French and English.
(c)	That Canadian trade be directed through Canadian ports and channels.
(d)	The appointment of a commissioner to make a complete study of West Indian and South American markets, and bring about the interchange of our northern products with those of the tropics, as this is the natural market for the surplus of our products of the farm, of the fisheries and of our forests.
(e)	The freeing of the Intercolonial Railway from the commission control and its restoration to Government administration in keeping with the pact of confederation.
(f)	The building of connecting links as feeders to railway main lines, thereby developing the agricultural, fisheries and the lumber industries of Canada, and particularly of the Maritime provinces.
Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that that is the platform upon which I stood in the last election, and I have no hesitation in stating that I believe my right hon. leader would subscribe to the essential part of that platform, which would be for the great advantage of this Dominion.

The House resumed at eight o'clock.

In connection with the charges made against us on the ground of sectional appeals during that campaign, of which I was speaking, let me quote a statement made by the Prime Minister of Canada at a public meeting held at Moncton in 1921, when he asked for the support of the electorate of the Maritime provinces on the following ground:
Mr. Mackenzie King said he deplored the fact that through not following the Laurier policy the result was that Canadian made goods were being exported to foreign ports and imports being brought in through foreign ports. The remedy to this condition of affairs was the return to Liberalism so that the Laurier policy might be furthered.
In view, Sir, of the claim that the Maritime provinces were not getting their just rights let me make a point clear to the House. The rights of the Maritime provinces have been talked about, and statements with respect of them have been published in the
press, nevertheless, I maintain there is no such thing as Maritime province rights, the rights that have been ignored and the conditions that exist in the Maritime provinces are not merely a matter of concern for the Maritime provinces, they are really of Dominion wide importance. Let me quote here, Sir, a statement copied from the Telegraph, St. John, which is not by any means favourable' to the opposition party in this House. This paper states that during the months of November and December, 1923, and of January, 1924, there was a wheat export through Portland, Maine, of 6,831,294 bushels compared with an export in the same three months of 454,168 bushels through the port of St. John, whereas not one solitary grain went through the port of Halifax. At the same time the Canadian Pacific Railway had shipped through the Canadian port of St. John 6,496,460 bushels of wheat. Hence it is that the clamour for provincial rights, or the sectional appeals of which we hear so much, come from the chief organs of the party of my hon. friends opposite.
I have here, Sir, a copy of the Moncton Transcript of 2nd April, 1993, when there was no probability of a by-election in the Maritime provinces. This is what the editor of the Transcript, the official organ of the Liberal party in that section of New Brunswick and a great supporter of the Secretary of State, said, quoting the figures of the President of the Canadian National Railways as to the increased revenue:
The public will not fail to note that according to Mr. Graham, the return of the Crowsnest grain rates cost the Canadian National $6,500,000 in revenue last year. That is to say, if these extra earnings had been available the operating surplus on the whole of the system would have been $10,600,000 instead of $4,100,000. In short the West was relieved to the extent of $6,500,000 which the rest of the country made up in the form of increased taxes.
Now, we say, Sir, that if that quotation is correct, and I believe it is correct, we were perfectly justified in saying in the Kent byelection that we could not, and we would not, permit the leader of this government to sacrifice the rights of any party in order to satisfy the Progressive party in this House.
Very affectionate.

If affectionate we must be, let us be affectionate to all parts of the country. I find that the rate on Nova Scotia coal from Montreal to Hamilton, a distance of 372 miles, is S3 per ton, while the rate on United States coal from Detroit to Montreal, 563 miles, is only $2.90 per ton, or 10 cents less for 190 miles greater distance. I ask my
The Address-Mr. Doucet

hon. friends who represent the constituencies of Cumberland and Pictou, and both ridings in Cape Breton, do they not believe with me that the coal industry of the Maritime provinces is not getting a fair deal at the hands of the railway board, but that United States bituminous coal receives certain concessions that we in the Maritime provinces do not enjoy?
It will be noted also that the rate of fishand these statements were made before the Railway Commission which met at Halifax a short time ago; and mark you, the express companies to-day are before the Railway-Commission and they are part and parcel of the Canadian National Railways-from Prince Rupert to Winnipeg, a distance of 1,758 miles, is $3.59 per 100 pounds, while the rate from Halifax to Winnipeg, a distance of 1,923 miles is $10.60 for the same weight. I wish to refer this item to the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) and to ask him to agree with me that the fishing industry of the Maritime provinces is not getting a fair deal.

How long have these rates
on fish been in existence? Were they not in existence quite a number of years before this government came into power?

I am not in a position to tell my hon. friend how long these rates have been in existence. But inasmuch as he himself admits that they are in existence to-day,
I say that, for the proper development of our fishing industry and of all other industries of the Maritime provinces, we come here not as whiners or beggars, but demanding our just rights. I am reminded that just before six o'clock I had laid bare before this House the campaign in which I ran as an independent candidate at the last election in 1921. During the recess my friends asked me what reasons I had for abandoning the independent idea this y-ear in the by-election. After the Liberal government came into power and after having reviewed their record of administration in this country, it did not take me long as it would not have taken any man with an ordinary amount of intelligence long, to come to the conclusion that the campaign of 1921 was a campaign of camouflage and a wholesale carnival of mendacity.

I would like to ask if the
Conservative government, prior to 1921 was satisfactory7 to the hon. member in his campaign.

I had really believed, and
I had been told that, a new member speaking in this House would not be subjected to interruptions. Of course, if interruptions

have to come, they will delay me a little longer than I expected. I really intended to close my remarks before six o'clock; but I was unable to do so on account of numerous interruptions which came from the official benches. I admit they were somewhat uneasy over those recent events in the Maritime provinces which were laid bare to-day in this House and which it was right that the whole country should know. We m the Maritime provinces are not beggars; but we contend that the government is committed, because in 1903 the act creating the National Transcontinental railway explicitly stated that all unrouted traffic should be routed through Canadian ports and entirely on Canadian territory, and that the through rate on export traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall at no time be greater via Canadian ports than via United States ports. I trust my hon. friend across the floor who interrupted me a minute ago will admit that that was passed in 1903, and by the self-same party which to-day has the reins of power. In the act of 1911, respecting the construction of the Canadian Northern railway, we find identically the same thing, and in 1911, the same party was in power. In 1914, in the act respecting the Canadian Northern railway system paragraph (a) of section 6 explicitly says the same thing. Therefore, the government of this country, having acquired those great railway systems, are to my mind and, I believe, in the mind of every other hon. member in this House, committed to carrying out to the letter the provisions of those statutes. The next fear is that we are selling too much again-for there is an impartiality about the fears of my right hon. and learned friend; first he fears we are selling too much, then he fears we are buying too much, and then he fears again that we are selling too much. Now he fears we are selling too many minerals in their raw state. He says:
But let us remember our duty is to see that these resources vouchsafed to us are to the utmost developed within the land that is our own, and to a minimum sent out of the country that other nations and other peoples may get the advantage of them.
This is the gospel of national selfishness- the narrow nationalist and protectionist view. It is the view of trade as being a contest, the view of trade which led the nations of Europe, prior to the war, to mark out in Africa and other less developed parts of the world "spheres of influence" so that they might control the resources and keep the markets for themselves. It was that spirit, as much as any other that led to the overwhelming calamity that broke on the world on the fourth of August, 1914. When we see that spirit demonstrated by the leader of a party, are we surprised that another prominent member of that party tells us that the life and death of the Founder of our religion is not an example to be followed but a warning to be avoided; and that another of his colleagues, not to be outdone, brings forward that quintessence of paganism which puts the rights and the advantages of one's country above morality; "May my country be always right, but my country right or wrong?" The national god set above morality! That would be the danger of allowing men holding such ideas to have control of the destinies of Canada, and care must be taken that our people understand these dangers and govern themselves accordingly.
Let me point out that the danger of this idea that a country with great natural resources has a right to play the dog in the manger, has a right to keep other nations from enjoying those resources, was noticed at the time the Peace treaty was made at Versailles, and it was endeavoured to be avoided in the Covenant of the League of Nations, for in that Covenant we find that the mandated territories, especially those in Africa, were placed under the more civilized powers, and it was provided in article 22 that in mandated territory the mandatory must allow equal opportunities for the trade and commerce of the members of the League.
But, there is another argument, and I think it is a just and reasonable one. What would

happen to us if the United States adopted that policy: We are to hold on to all our natural resources and only export in a finished state what we want to sell? What would happen to us if the United States adopted that policy in regard to cotton? By the constitution of that country export duties are prohibited, but we have seen recently that the Americans can amend their constitution. Suppose they amended it in that fashion, suppose they put on a heavy export duty or a prohibition on the export of raw cotton, what would happen to our cotton mills? Last year we imported cotton to the value of $47,000,000 in round figures, of which $30,000,000, or two-thirds, represented raw cotton. Well, where would the Dominion Textile and the Canadian Cottons be if they were unable to get their raw cotton free into this country? It is a serious thing to think of, but it is a poor rule that does not work both ways, and it is egregious folly to propose to follow a course of conduct which, if followed by one's neighbour, may hurt you very much indeed. Coal is in the same situation. In 1923 we imported $43,750,000 worth of anthracite coal and $48,500,000 worth of bituminous coal. This coal was imported because it served our interest best to buy it in the United States. The price of coal is largely determined by the freight rate. Of course, we have immense quantities of coal both in Alberta and in Nova Scotia, but the question is, how expedient it is to haul coal those very long distances; and, of course, it would be a bad thing for us, I take it, if export duties were placed upon coal by the United States. As far as anthracite coal is concerned, a few years ago we had in Canada a shortage of coal. He laid down this principle, as being the true principle of protection as taught by Sir John A. This is about the most reasonable of all the protectionist arguments, and if it worked that way in practice there might be something to be said for it. But the protests which we have throughout the country to-day is one of the best evidences of how difficult it is, after the duty is once put on, to have it reduced or taken off.

Bis second argument was that the industry was becoming more and more centralized into a few hands. Is that true to-day? We come now to the question of woollen importations. Woollen importations from Great Britain have increased by $4,000,000. So that, taking them all together raw wool, noils, tops and yams-these three raw materials for our Canadian mills-constitute just half of the increase. But there has been another result of this increase of woollens into Canada. The result has been that the consumers of this country are getting their socks and their stockings cheaper than they were getting them a few years ago; and I think that the interests of the men, and the women and the children who wear stockings and socks in Canada have really more claim on this, or any other government, than has the particular interest that manufacture such things. Then just before I pass from the question of knitted goods, woollen goods, I would make this observation. It may be that some of the smaller mills have gone out of business. I should like to turn to the address delivered by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler). I regret that he is not in his place to-night. I should like to congratulate him-and my words, of course, will reach him in due course-upon the very able presentation which he made of the financial condition of the country, a presentation which showed immense research, immense labour, and which was most attractively set forth in this House. As to his remarks upon the trade question, I do not find myself in such complete accord. He stated:
We are not a sufficiently self-contained nation. We should be self-dependent. We should not import so much foodstuffs or so much manufactured goods as we do.
As to foodstuffs, I have already wearied the House with statistics in connection with the observation made along the same lines by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen). As to manufactured goods, what appears to be forgotten by the hon. member is this, that unless we are prepared to receive largely in manufactured goods the price of our premanufactured goods the price of our exports of natural products, I, for the life of me, do not know how we are going to get paid for our exports.

What kind of credit would the hon. gentleman think would be made available by the payment of our annual indebtedness out of this country, a very large amount of which indebtedness is held in England, some $260,000,000?

No doubt we have an annual indebtedness to be paid and some of it is due in England. I would imagine that a 'great proportion of our debt which has been due in England, has already been transferred to the United States. I have no need to press the point, because I observe the-hon. member agrees with me. I doubt whether we have a great deal due in England now, though we have a certain amount, and of course Great Britain owes us on national account a considerable amount of money, some $10,000,000. I am afraid she will. As a matter of fact, I do not believe our farmer friends are going to ship grain which they do not get paid for, and I am sure our millers are not going to ship flour unless they get paid for it.
Has my hon. friend made any calculation as to the amount of the annual indebtedness of Canada?

I have not made any calculation as to the exact amount of our indebtedness in Great Britain, and I do not think it could be made, for the reason that a great deal of our securities that represent debts which we contracted in days gone by through the issue of bonds in London, went over to the United States when Great Britain was borrowing heavily from the United States during the war, and also that vast quantities were bought back by ourselves. I remember when my hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) was Minister of Finance, he placed a sort of voluntary embargo against the re-importation of our Canadian securities from London for the purpose, he said, of maintaining exchange rates.

My hon. friend is quite wrong about that. It was not for the purpose of maintaining exchange rates; it was for quite a different reason, but that is an extraneous matter. Would my hon. friend give us his idea, as a financial expert, what the sum really is? I am speaking, not about our indebtedness in England alone, but about our foreign indebtedness. It has been placed at various sums. The lowest I know of is

$260,000,000 a year on interest account, whether he accepts that or not.

I cannot accept that without full opportunity to examine into the whc,le situation. The point I wish to make is an<l I do not think it can be gainsaid

that when we export goods from Canada, we have to be prepared to take payment for those goods in large measure in manufactured articles coming from abroad. I quite agree with the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) that we owe money abroad, but I cannot say how much money we owe abroad. I think in view of the transfers of securities from the Old Country to the United States and to ourselves during and since the war, any estimate made is merely an estimate and cannot be accepted as definite, though I do not doubt for a moment that we still owe a considerable amount of money outside of this country. But I would say that it was mostly in the hands of United States, and not of British, investors; and if we are going to continue to send vast quantities of our raw materials and of our manufactured natural products, such as flour, to the markets of Britain and Europe we must be prepared to take payment in goods. Now, how do nations adjust their trade balances? In days gone by, when the balance was only a little one way or the other, it was done in gold. But now the export of gold from one country to another is practically forbidden. A nation may pay in services for the goods which it receives, and no doubt a certain amount of our raw materials and our flour which we send to Great Britain is paid for by insurance and shipping services which the people of the Old Land give to Canada. There is however no question that in the ultimate analysis the great medium of payment for our goods which we ship is goods of a different sort which we receive in return. The point I want to make is that you cannot interfere with the flow of goods into a country without interfering at the same time with the export of goods from that country. That is not merely a principle'that is current in the classrooms of college professors of political economy, it is the foundation stone of international banking and is a fact that is known to every international banker in the world. What do the ships carry which we see leaving Montreal? Sometimes you will see a tramp steamer which is loaded entirely with wheat, carrying nothing else,-it may have a few deals spread here and there in order to prevent the wheat from shifting on the stormy sea. But the typical cargo, as I was informed by one of the head shipping men in

The Address-Mr. McMaster
Montreal when I was there last week end, is wheat, cheese and packed meats from Chicago or Canada. That is the typical cargo of the liners leaving Montreal; and on the ships coming in we get all sorts of goods from the Old Country.
I do not want to dwell too long on this point. Let me take another. Can protection increase employment in the lump or as a whole? It cannot. And this is the reason. It is quite possible that if you protect one industry you may give more employment to men engaged in that particular line than you would if you allowed matters to follow their course. But you cannot increase employment as a whole, because when you get goods into the country they are paid for by something you produce in the country itself, and the production of those goods gives as much employment as if you manufactured or produced what is imported. The only difference is this, that where you allow trade to flow freely the labour and capital of the country will flow into the channels which will produce the greatest wealth instead of being diverted, as they often are, into lines of activity which really are an economic waste so far as the national wealth is concerned. Let me give two examples. Before the war a certain British shipbuilder tendered for six ships to be built in Great Britain. He was able to tender lower than anyone else because he could buy his steel very cheaply in Belgium. But, you may say, the steel workers of Great Britain were deprived of the work of making that steel which would go into the ship. That argument is unsound, because the ships would never have been built in Great Britain unless the shipbuilder had been able to get cheap steel from Belgium. The ships would never have been built, and neither the shipbuilders in Great Britain nor the steelmakers in Britain would have had any work. But being able to get cheap steel from Belgium the shipbuilder was in a position to give employment to labour in Great Britain; and while the steelmakers there had nothing to do with * that particular order they no doubt were working on some other order.
. There is a famous economist in the United States, William F. Culbertson, who is on the tariff board of the American government. He cites a case to show how import duties will interfere with trade and business, and therefore with labour. In the production of high grade steel a manufacturer must have a substantial supply of tungsten, chromium and manganese. A duty is imposed on these minerals by the tariff law of the United States of 1922. It therefore became necessary
to give compensatory duties to protect the maker of this high grade steel in the American market; and as far as the American market was concerned he was almost as well off as before. But the manufacturer, when he went into the foreign market, was at a disadvantage as against the steel manufacturer who was able to get tungsten, chromium and manganese free of customs duties. In that way protection must always reduce labour in so far as it prevents labour from working for a larger market, it is bound to increase the cost of production. Of course, the fear that lower duties must result in unemployment disappears when one grasps the way in which international trade is carried on.
Perhaps I might be allowed at this point to refer to an observation made by the hon. member in connection with preferences. He said in the course of his remarks that we gave preferences to Great Britain because we wished to increase our exports to that country and hoped that at some time or other Great Britain would give us preference in her markets. I do not believe that was the reason why preferences were given. They were given, to a certain extent at least, as a matter of profound and clever political strategy. That is something that may possibly be advisable at times, although I am not particularly fond of it. For years before the election of 18% our Tory friends carried on a campaign of waving the old flag. In 1891 Sir John A. Macdonald said:	"A British
subject I was bom; a British subject I will die," and he denounced the Grits because they proposed reciprocity with the United States. In 18% the flag was waved, as it has been on some occasions since-the same tactics have been pursued since that time. What did the Minister of Finance do in 1897? The Liberal party had promised a reduction of duties, and so he reduced the duties by giving a substantial British preference, thus rather spiking the guns of his political opponents who had wreathed themselves about with the Union Jack and pretended1 to be the sole depositors of Imperial sentiment and British loyalty. But even there the matter was done not altogether to my liking, because some of the duties were raised before the preference was given. Preferences may have their place where two protectionist nations decide to move towards free trade, and each one gives to the other a certain facility in his market. It is a sort of reciprocity. It may be, and I think is, justified where a country moving from a protectionist status to a freer trade status gives

manufacturer. Now, my hon. friend, when I was trying to lead him into a statement in that regard, failed to be led, so I had to go to the figures to make my proof. I find that for the last calendar year the dutiable goods coming from Great Britain amounted to $125,000,000 and that the dutiable goods coming from the United States amounted to almost three times that sum, $361,000,000 while from the United States we imported just about four times as much goods as we did from Great Britain-in fact, fibres and textiles are the only manufactured goods in which the United Kingdom is in any way a competitor with the United States in our markets, that is, as reflected by the trade returns. Of fibres and textiles, $74,000,000 worth came from the United Kingdom and $78,000,000 from the United States, and as to all the rest-iron and its products, nonferrous metals, non-metallic minerals, and chemical products-we find that the amounts received from the United Kingdom are trifling in comparison to the amounts received from the United States. So I think I can say with a fair degree of accuracy that the great competitor for our manufactures is not the United Kingdom, not France, not Italy, not the countries of Asia, but the United States, and that wages in the United States are if anything higher than in Canada. So that I think the maintenance of tariff for the purpose of protecting us from cheap labour falls to the ground.
And after all, does cheap labour actually involve low labour costs? Not at all. Very often the best-paid labour is the cheapest in the long run. In countries like the United States and Canada the efficient well fed and ambitious workman, although paid a higher wage than the workman of the same class in Great Britain, France or Italy, who has not the idea that he has to "ca' canny" or go easy but believes he should do the best he can for his employer, that he should be prepared to mind as many machines as it is reasonable for him to mind, the workman not imbued with the idea of going as slowly as he can but with the idea of doing as much as he can-that man is in the long run the cheap workman, and he is much cheaper at a high wage than the man with less ambition and less capacity at a much lower wage. And then, of course, we must distinguish between nominal wages and real wages. Protection does not, in my humble opinion, raise real wages. It may possibly, by raising the cost of living, bring about a certain increase of the nominal wages, but not of the real wages. What are the facts? Does protection increase real wages? I take it that it does not. Let me make my point clear.
'Mr. McMaster.]
Protection cannot increase the aggregate wealth of any people. Protection is a tax; protection is a method whereby the government undertakes to direct the labour or capital of the country into one channel rather than into another. Now, the greatest aggregate wealth will be created if labour and capital are allowed freely to find, and they will do so, the channels *which will give the greatest economic return. Therefore, under free trade will you get the greatest aggregate of wealth.
Now, what are your wages? Wages are the reward which labour is able to extract from capital. Does it do that better under protection or under free trade? What does protection do? Protection has a tendency to make capital coalesce into larger and larger groups; the larger the group the more power it has. Where do we find the strongest labour unions -in the United States under protection, or in Great Britain under free trade? The fact that we have a Labour government in England today I think adequately answers that question.
I am afraid I have delayed the House for a very long time, and I must ask the pardon of the members for doing so. I have endeavoured to point out the reasons why I believe that the protectionist appeal is a mistaken appeal for this country. The protectionist is fighting in this country against the facts of nature and the facts of geography. We cannot be a self-dependent country. We have got practically only one climate; we are a fairly narrow country, that is, the inhabited part of our country stretching along the northern confines of the United States. We need to trade freely. We need to have the labour and the capital of our country directed into those channels where the greatest economic wealth can be afforded. I do not know how we are to support the economic burdens which we have upon us unless we follow that policy. I ask no government to do anything of an extreme nature, but I do ask this government to see that when they place laws on the statute book reducing the duties, those laws are not defeated by regulations. Let me give just a few examples. A client of mine was accustomed to bring in waxed paper from the Old Land for the purpose of wrapping up his loaves; he was a baker. On that wrapping paper was his name and trade-mark. For some time he brought it in under a 22J per cent duty. You would have thought that was a high enough duty, but what happened? The Department of Customs declared that was advertising matter. It was no more advertising matter than his carts bearing the same label were advertising matter when they went round the streets of Westmount delivering his

The Address-Mr. McQuarrie
bread. But that was regarded as advertising matter and taxed at a much higher rate.
I have a letter in my pocket from a man in the western part of Canada protesting that when he brought in apples that were taxed at the rate of 30 cents a box, which had been bought in the open market and on which no special discount was given, the Customs made an arbitrary ruling that these had been bought too cheaply and that he must pay an extra 16| cents per box, which brought up the duty on apples to a 50 per cent ad valorem rate.
Could my hon. friend tell me.the date of that letter? When did this happen?

The letter is dated
March 7, 1924, and reads:
During the month of February we purchased several cars of apples from Yakima, Washington State, U.S.A., at 90 cents and some at 85 cents per box F.O.B. there. The duty on these apples was assessed at the rate of 90 cents per barrel or 30 cents per box; but on the top of this the Customs under the Dumping Act have added a further charge of 16J cents per box. They claim we bought the apples less than they were worth, although these apples were offered and are still being offered freely at same prices.
What the Customs should realize is that they are an organization for collecting revenue on things that come in, not for the purpose, under various pretexts, of keeping things out. I ask for nothing unreasonable. I know that when a country has followed for many years a certain system, that system must be changed with care and discretion. I believe that there are no people in this country whose desires are other than mine in regard to the trade question. We want action; we want prudent action; but we want action visible to the naked eye. I speak for myself; I have no right to speak for any other; but I confidently believe that I represent the feelings
of a large number of people in this country, and the measure of the support which such people will give to this government will be in proportion to the spirit of true liberalism and of true progress which it demonstrates in the difficult task of governing and leading this country forward to a better and a finer condition of affairs.

As I listened to the remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. McMaster) I wondered if the government could actually be so unkind when the Redistribution Bill comes up again as to abolish the constituency of Brome; and in that eventuality would it be possible for the hon. member to find another constituency?
Lots of them.
It would be a great loss to this House and to the country if the hon. gentleman had to leave us.
No danger.

We cannot blame the government for wishing to decapitate the hon. gentleman, nor can you blame the hon. gentleman for leaving the government side of the House. The hon. gentleman is a very eloquent and convincing speaker, but so far as I can see he is not able to convince anyone but himself. Hence his position of splendid isolation at the tail-end of the House. He was not able to convince the cabinet, nor was he able to convince anyone on his side of the House. I doubt very much whether he will be able to convince anyone on the benches immediately adjoining his seat, where the Labour party sits, nor on the benches to my left; for if he did the only effect would be for them to vote against the government, which I think is practically impossible.
May I be permitted, Mr. Speaker, to add my words of congratulation to the mover (Mr. Kelly) and the seconder (Mr. Lapierre) of the Address. With a great many of the things that they said I am, of course, unable to agree, for obvious reasons. One thing I remarked while the mover was speaking and that was the vociferous applause of the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell), who seemed to take quite a fatherly interest in the Address.
May I also express regret at the absence of the Minister of Finance who commands the respect and admiration, I think, not only of all the members of the House but of the people of Canada as a whole. I think it is a distinct loss to Canada that he is unable to occupy his position in this Chamber during the present session.
I regret also that the former Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) is not able to occupy the position which he used to hold. I must say that I do not regret that the former Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) is now Minister of Justice. He took an interest in his late department, and I have no doubt he will take an equal interest in die Justice department which in my opinion requires some attention. In regard to the former Minister of Justice there is a story current which may or may not have any foundation; I will give it for what it is worth. It is said that the late Minister of Justice was asked if he had given up his position because he was really ill, or if there were other reasons for his retirement. He said that while it was quite true he was far from well, he was not as sick as the Liberal party.

May I also be permitted to congratulate the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Doucet) upon his maiden speech. I think he did splendidly. He is an asset to the Conservative party, and I predict that he is the forerunner of a great many more of his race who will, in a comparatively short time, line themselves up with the Conservative party. I have been wondering about something in connection with the hon. member for Lot-biniere (Mr. Vien). We saw in the press not very long ago that the hon. gentleman had been appointed Deputy Minister of National Defence and we thought-at least I did when I came down here-that congratulations were due him. Now I find the newspaper forecast has not been realized; surprising to say the 'hon. gentleman is still in his place in this Chamber. I have been trying to account for this and am wondering whether it is possible the government has come to such a state that it is afraid to open a constituency in Quebec. It looks very much as though that might be the case, and I think, particularly after what has happened in Halifax and Kent that is the explanation.
My congratulations are also due to the new Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin). I was rather surprised to hear that he bad been placed in that important position because, so far as I was aware, he had had nothing to do with fisheries up to the date of his assuming cabinet rank and there are certain hon. gentlemen opposite who have taken a very active interest in the fisheries. My mind dwells particularly on the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) who was the great critic on fishery questions when he was in opposition, and has been chairman of the Committee on Fisheries during the present parliament. I have been wondering whether there was a reason for the failure to promote the hon. member for Lunenburg, and thinking that perhaps the government was afraid to open up that constituency also. There is another hon. member of this House who might have been appointed to that position and that is the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork). He, of course, is from British Columbia and has been very much interested in the fisheries there for a great many years. Beyond all doubt British Columbia is entitled to further cabinet representation. Under the late government British Columbia was represented in two important portfolios, namely, Agriculture, and Trade and Commerce. It would have been a fit and proper thing on the part of the present government to have chosen an additional cabinet minister for 
British Columbia, but it did not do so. The reason, perhaps, is the same as in the other cases-the government is afraid to open a British Columbia constituency. I am very doubtful indeed whether it would be possible for this government to elect even a cabinet minister in that province.
Sir, as I have already said we have a new Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I had the pleasure of a few minutes' conversation with him the other night, and he very kindly consented to give me an audience so that I might go into matters relating to the British Columbia fisheries with him. I think from the attitude he adopted towards me that night, that we shall find him a man Who is willing to see what can be done in his department. British Columbia as hon. members are aware, is a province where the fisheries are important and require, and should receive, consideration. There are a number of matters which are entitled to consideration and I think should be looked into. I had the privilege of discussing them with the present Minister of Justice, and I think he could advise the new Minister of Marine and Fisheries that the British Columbia fisheries should be looked into. There is, for instance, the Fraser river which was the greatest salmon fishery stream at one time. On the Fraser river in 1913 something over 700,000 eases of sockeye salmon, perhaps the best grade of salmon on the world's markets were packed. But there has been a falling off in the pack. We have big years every four years. The pack in 1913 was one of the big years. In 1921 the last big year only 50,000 cases of sockeye salmon were packed on the Fraser. Sockeye salmon is worth approximately $15 a case. So the new minister will comprehend immediately that the situation requires looking into. If it is possible to do anything, no time should be lost. I am convinced that something can be done. The most important feature is to continue negotiations with the authorities of the state of Washington. They are also suffering from the depletion of the fisheries in the same proportion as we are.
I would like to see the new minister take the question of the Fraser river fisheries up with the board of the state of Washington and see if something can be done. An arrangement might have been made with the authorities of that state whereby the Fraser river would be closed to sockeye fishing for a number of years. They were willing to adopt a close season for a period of years, but they would not say what would 10 p.m. happen at the conclusion of that term, and they were not prepared

The Address-Mr. McQuarrie
to give any assurance they would not again resort to the old methods which were calculated to deplete the supply. If that means simply restoring the sockeye salmon for the Americans there does not seem to be very much in the proposition. We would like to have an arrangement whereby, at the end of a closed period, the Americans would agree to abide by certain rules and regulations similar to our own. It may not be necessary to close the river entirely for that period, and I do not think it is or will be. As a matter of fact, I can state to the minister, that all the fishing interests in British Columbia, the canning associations, the fishermen and the businessmen are all agreed-they can get together on it-that no sockeye fishing should be allowed prior to the 1st August in any year. That would give the early fish, the ones which go up to the upper regions of the river, which have been absolutely depleted, a chance to ascend the stream and get to those spawning grounds. That might be tried out, and I may say that that opinion has been expressed by some very eminent authorities on fisheries.
There are a number of other matters in connection with the fisheries of British Columbia. I have placed on the order paper certain questions as to the very important recommendations contained in the report of the British Columbia Fisheries Commission, 1922. I am asking if the government intends to do anything to give effect to those recommendations. I hope the minister will look mto the matter, and I think if he studies the question, he will come to the conclusion that those recommendations should be carried out.
I should like for a moment, to refer to one feature of the address delivered by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork) in this debate. That is as to the central organization in British Columbia. I must state positively that . I cannot agree in any particular with the hon. member for Skeena. I think it would be a mistake to do away with the central organization. I put it to you, Mr. Speaker, whether any business concern, with its head office in the East and having a branch or wanting to do business in British Columbia, would not establish a central organization there, a British Columbia office, as it were, which would administer, to a certain extent, the British Columbia business? I think that would be the case rather than that the concern should have representatives in the important cities and districts of British Columbia and have no central organization whatever. The desire of the hon. member for Skeena for economy in this connection would
not be attained. He has stated that we might save some $50,000 by doing away with that central organization. I do not believe that. There are three districts, and he proposes that each one of those three districts should communicate with Ottawa directly. I believe that instead of having the expense of one organization there as you have now, you would have the expense of three, and the total cost to the country would be thereby multiplied and not decreased. There is a suggestion which I would like to make to the minister and which, it seems to me, is worthy of consideration, if he desires to effect economy in the fisheries administration of British Columbia. Prior to very recently, the central organization in British Columbia was located at New Westminster. They have there a government building, a fisheries building, with ample accommodation for the office. The office was moved to Vancouver where space was rented in one of the large blocks at quite a large rental. If the minister will return that central office to New Westminster, not only might the rental be saved, but I think the staff might be decreased. That is to say, you might use the staff at present in New Westminster with the central organization and thereby possibly eliminate some of the employees. But in any event, by returning the central organization to New Westminster, you would effect a very considerable saving and no one would be hurt. It takes only about twenty-five minutes to go from New Westminster to Vancouver, and there is a first class pavement all the way. There is no reason why the cannery men whose head offices are located at Vancouver, when they are required to do business with the central office, could not either telephone or come over to New Westminster. The really serious situation in connection with British Columbia at present exists on the Fraser river. New Westminster is right on the Fraser river, and it seems to me that that is the proper place for the fisheries office to be where it had been for many years. The offices were taken away without any previous intimation to myself, although I happened to be the member for that constituency. I later on objected, and in that objection I received the support of all the members from British Columbia, with the exception of the members for Vancouver, who took no active part at all in the matter. I think the same condition would prevail now and that almost complete unanimity would be found amongst the members from British Columbia on the question of returning the fisheries office to New Westminster.
The Address-Mr. McQuarrie

In referring to the Fraser river, might I also touch on another matter which was brought up by the hon. member for Skeena, that is in connection with grain elevators? I listened with great interest to what he said about Prince Rupert, and I am not going to contest any of his statements in regard to the attractions which are offered by Prince Rupert as a shipping point fcr grain. But I say that New Westmmstei is on the main line of the Canadian National railways. The Fraser river is the first point where grain could be loaded on boats. The Fraser has every facility for the location of grain elevators. The Canadian National Railways, if the question were left with them, would express themselves, no doubt very freely, in favour of locating elevators on the Fraser river. The Canadian Pacific Railway has already said the same thing; it has done more than that; it has acquired large tracts of land on the Pitt river which is a tributary of the Fraser river at Port Coquitlam not very far removed from the Fraser river. My hon. friends from the prairie provinces will be interested in this because it is a matter of economy, a matter of expense, pure and simple, a matter of cost, cost of transportation. We had a visit this year from a number of our Progressive friends who inspected the Fraser river and its facilities. The question is one of shipping grain at the least possible expense, and I need only point out that to take the grain from New Westminster to Burrard Inlet at Vancouver costs something like $15 a car. Besides that, there is a good deal of congestion, and it may be difficult to obtain sites there. In any event, the sites would be very expensive. There is, on the other hand, by locating the elevators at New Westminster, a saving of $15 a car. It may be said by the shippers that the railway companies will have to bear that expense. You know what that means. If means that although the railway company bears the initial expense, at some time or other, eventually, someone else will have to pay, and it will have to come out of the traffic. I suggest that the Fraser river be given a trial. I know that this to a large extent is a matter for private enterprise, but we are hoping that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King, Kootenay), who has interested himself in the Fraser river, will continue the work which has been carried on there for some time in connection with the channel of the river. That channel has been greatly improved; we have had quite a good deal of shipping in the last couple of years, 
and the ships of the Canadian Merchant Marine and of other lines are coming there pretty frequently for lumber. The Fraser river is the centre of the lumber industry of British Columbia, about one-third of the lumber out in the province being cut by the mills on that river. The business is there, and I respectfully ask that the Minister of Public Works continue the work he has been doing.
I quite agree with other hon. gentlemen who have spoken about the necessity for strict economy, and it seems to me that we might begin the practice of economy in this House. In any event I think it would be advisable that the session should be as short as possible consistent with the business that comes before the House. I was pleased to hear from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) that the cost in connection with parliament was not so large as had been reported; but still we all know that it costs a good deal to keep this House going. I suggest that m order to reduce the length of the session we might meet each day at 2.30 instead of 3 o'clock in the afternoon. I can see no reason why that should not be done. Personally, I would go so far as to advocate meeting at 2 o'clock, but that perhaps might be inconvenient for the cabinet. I do think, however, that we might try 2.30 and save half an hour each day; over a period of four or five months that would represent a considerable economy of time.
I would call the attention of my hon. friends to my left to a statement made recently by the Right Hon. William M. Hughes, former Premier of Australia, who said that three parties were a luxury which no country could afford. I think the Progressive group might take that suggestion into consideration. They could divide things up, some of them coming over here and others going on the opposite side of the House. I do not suppose that they would all go over to the other side; but when they are voting with the government, or at least the great majority of them, there is no reason why they should not be on the opposite side, thus dispensing with this "luxury". I think that sane economy should be practised, and not false economy which would tend to retard the development of the country, I regret the policy of the government which has resulted in the discontinuance of federal aid to highway construction. A great deal of,very valuable work was done by means of that grant, and when we realize the fact that tourists who come to this country leave many millions of dollars, and that many millions more would be spent in the country if we had good roads, I think
The Address-Mr. McQuarrie
the government should see the advisability of reconsidering its pi licy and of again doing something to assist in the construction of highways. It is also a matter for regret that the government has discontinued the aid to agricultural education. That was something that was doing considerable good. In our part of the country a great deal had been accomplished through the women's institutes and other organizations which were supported from this grant. I am very sorry indeed that the government saw fit to discontinue this aid.
Let me refer for a moment to the question of old age pensions. I think the time has arrived when this country should do something in this regard. I shall not go into the question at great length to-night, but we have seen how the matter works in other countries that are smaller and less prosperous than our own, and it seems to me that the time has come when it should be seriously considered by the government of this country. While I am on this subject I might also mention another of great importance; I have reference to the grant to the Victorian Order of Nurses. That grant has been $5,000 a year, which, in my opinion, is a disgracefully small sum for a country like this to contribute to an organization of that kind. The health of the people is a matter of vital importance; it is the most important thing that public money can be expended upon. If hon. members had the privilege of following one of the Victorian Order *Nurses on her rounds he would see what a splendid, noble, heroic work these nurses are doing. He would find such a nurse going to homes that would not otherwise receive the attention of any nurse; he would find her going into homes where the people could not afford to pay for the services of a nurse; he would find that the organization was doing a great deal of charitable work. "In these circumstances I think it would be a small thing to the country, and the increased taxation would be hardly appreciable, if that grant were made twenty-five thousand dollars instead of five thousand. The committees throughout Canada, working under the patronage of Her Excellency, are doing very valuable work voluntarily, without remuneration, and they are having a hard time. I seriously urge the government to take the matter into consideration.
Now I come to the Civil Service. There is no doubt in my mind that care should be exercised in the dismissals that are made in the Civil Service, because it is a matter of much importance that efficiency be not impaired. I think that a fair living wage should be provided for all who are retained in the 23
service. I do not believe in keeping anyone in the service who is not doing his or her work or who is not of value to the country. I do say, however, that those who are retained should receive a fair living wage, and they should be decently treated just as the employees of an ordinary employer would be treated. The stability of salaries should be established; I do not believe in the principle of bonuses at all. To my mind it is a pernicious system, and more than that it seems to be-in fact I know it is-unsatisfactory to the employees themselves, for they do not know where they stand. I have seen recommendations which have been made by the Amalgamated Civil Servants of Canada to the government, and I do not think these recommendations are unreasonable. They ask for a salary revision and I think it should be granted; they request that the whole matter be taken up and salaries revised and put upon a fair and reasonable basis. Then there is the matter of superannuation. It is a most unfair thing in my opinion, that a man or woman who has served the country for a number of years, should be turned out upon the street without consideration. We should have superannuation, and I hope the government will do something in that direction,
I agree with those who say that taxation must be reduced, and there are ways of doing it which probably will be discovered by the new Auditor General or by the cabinet themselves. At least I hope so. I think the sales tax should be revised, because unquestionably it is not equitable in its operation. I will give an example of this in connection with our lumbering industry. A tremendous export business has grown up in British Columbia lumber, but those engaged in it are up against the sales tax. For instance, if a saw-milling company receives an order, say, from the Canadian Pacific Railway, for a shipment of lumber, the price will be quoted plus 8 per cent sales tax; if the railway company goes to a licensed wholesaler, the price quoted will be plus 3 per cent sales tax; if an order is given by the Dominion government-and a good deal of lumber is used there by the Public Works department as the minister is aware-the Dominion government has to pay a 6 per cent sales tax, while if the provincial government is the buyer no tax is payable at all. Without going into further detail, I need only say that this condition of affairs is not good business, and there must be a revision of the tax.
Then the income tax should be reduced. I would suggest that life insurance premiums be exempted. I think it is a wise policy to



The Address-Mr. McQuarrie
encourage our people to provide protection for their families, and I am not a life insurance agent; I do not need to argue the question. In the province of British Columbia there is an exemption for premiums of life insurance on the life of the taxpayer "not to exceed one-sixth of the total of the gioss annual income of the taxpayer, if paid, receipts therefor to be produced to the assessor on demand." That has been the British Columbia law for some time, and is, I understand, also the law in England.
As to the tariff, I wish first of all to state that we in British Columbia are diiectly as well as indirectly interested in the prosperity of the prairie provinces. They are our neighbours and we are affected immediately by conditions there. In fact, our seaports are claimed by the people of those provinces as their own. The grain from all of Alberta and a great part of Saskatchewan will in a comparatively short time go out by the Pacific coast ports. Estimates have been made by those who know what they are talking about that inside of five years 200,000,000 bushels of grain will be exported through the Pacific ports. Hon. members will appreciate what that means to us. Therefore I say advisedly that we are interested in the prairie provinces in more ways than one. When the farmers on the prairies make, money they come to British Columbia to reside, and thereupon their ideas on the tariff completely change-as a general rule they become good Conservatives. I know of them, men who had been heads of locals and had occupied other positions of prominence in the prairie provinces, supported me during the last election. We are glad to have them come to our province, and if any -method can be devised to revise the tariff in such a way as to benefit the prairies without seriously hurting us, why every man and woman in British Columbia will hold up both hands for it. We are prepared to co-operate with the farmers of the prairies. Therefore I hope some solution of this difficult question will be arrived at.
On the 10th instant I asked the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Graham) a question in regard to the American tariff on Canadian wheat, and I will read the question and answer as they appear in Hansard of that date:
Mr. W. G. McQuarrie (New Westminster): Might I ask if the government contemplates taking any action, by way of retaliation or otherwise, in regard to the proposed increase in the United States tariff against Canadian wheat and wheat products?
Hon. members will note that I said, "by way of retaliation or otherwise."
[Mr. McQuarrie. 1
Hon. G. P. Graham (Acting Prime Minister): "Retaliation" is a bad word to use in business, if the object of trade is to make a profit. I would not like to say that the government had even been considering retaliation.
Well, apparently they have not been considering anything else in that connection. That is the great trouble with this government-they are inactive, they do nothing.
The member for Vancouver did not say so.

You need not take my word for it. I can quote to you from a good Liberal British Columbia newspaper on the subject-a newspaper which, as far as I know, has always supported this government. This is a short extract from the Vancouver Sun of the 17th January last, and is from the clever pen of John P. McConnell:
What is the outstanding fact in Canadian politics to-day? "Inaction of the government," is the answer.
Inaction in progressive legislation, inaction in carrying out promised programmes of development, inaction in reducing taxation, inaction in bringing in immigration, inaction in reducing emigration, inaction in promised tariff reforms, inaction in reducing the expenditures to meet revenues, inaction in reducing the national debt- everywhere you look you see a dreary, silent wilderness of dormant inaction.
This is the most general complaint I hear in Toronto and Montreal by both friends and enemies of the government, in business and political circles.
Inactivity, smug complacence of the government in face of crying demands of the country, are getting on the nerves of the business community. . .
Recent happenings in the East do not tend to increase confidence either in the government's intentions or ability to remedy matters.
That is the trouble in connection with the tariff. In British Columbia, in my constituency for instance, we are very much interested in the tariff. I can tell my Progressive friends that I represent something like 20,000 farmers as well as about 25,000 other people. In my constituency there is the best ' farming land in British Columbia, the delta of the Fraser river. We produce almost anything that could be produced anywhere, with the possible exception of tropical fruits. We have to admit that "we have no bananas," but otherwise we can produce anything. It is a great dairying district, and besides we produce hay and oats, vegetables of all kinds, and fruits. We have the greatest poultry business of any part of Canada, I suppose. We are right up against this question of the tariff, there is no doubt about it. I do not think my Progressive friends would be anxious to injure us, except perhaps, to benefit themselves in their own respective districts.
The member for Yale (Mr. MacKelvie) has spoken about fruit; I am interested in fruit, too. We grow in my constituency and

The Address-Mr. McQuarrie
in the adjoining constituency large quantities particularly of small fruits and I can corroborate everything the hon. gentleman said in that connection. Let me just mention one point in connection with eggs. Mind you, we are right there beside the border, and running through, but of -course not all in, my constituency for a distance of 2,000 miles, from Vancouver to San Diego, California, there is the Pacific highway, a paved road all the way. Every day, I was almost going to say every hour, big truckloads of produce grown in the United States come into our markets vi.a that road and the result is very hurtful indeed to our farmers. I have here an editorial from the same paper that I referred to a moment ago, the Vancouver Sun, dealing with the subject of eggs, and if the House will permit me, I will read it. It was published on the third of this month and it 6ays:
Failure of the Ottawa government to impose a reciprocal tariff on eggs entering Canada from the United States is having a depressing and, in some instances, an almost calamitous effect on the poultry industry of British Columbia. .
Both in point of quality and quantity this province has become one of the chief egg-producing centres of the North American continent.
According to official record of performance figures, the percentage of birds qualified in British Columbia as producers of 150 eggs and over, has increased from 21.2 in 1920, 39.3 in 1921, 47.8 in 1922 to 68.5 in 1923. Annual percentages for the rest of Canada are, 11.9 in 1920, 19.5 in 1921, 19.8 in 1922 and 30.1 in 1923.
British Columbia birds qualified as producers of 225 eggs and over, have increased from 2.2 in 1920 to 18.9 in 1923. The increase in this class for the rest of Canada has only been 1.5 in 1920 to 2.5 in 1923.
British Columbia, therefore, is Canada's chief poultry centre. Legislation in regard to the Canadian poultry business should be based on British Columbia records as a standard.
But instead of encouraging and nourishing the British Columbia poultry industry, existing Canadian tariff laws consistently throw business into the hands of American competitors.
The Eastern Canadian market is flooded at present with American eggs that gain entry to the country on the comparatively negligible tariff impost of 3 cents a dozen. Considering the difference in transportation costs, British Columbia producers cannot begin to compete in the Eastern market under such a handicap.
Moreover, the opportunity to recoup this loss in the New York market is obviated by the fact that Canadian egg exporters are faced with an 8-cent duty when they attempt to ship into the United States.
British Columbia poultrymen, therefore, are shut out of American markets by high American tariffs and shut out of Canadian markets by American competition fostered by low Canadian tariffs.
Until the Canadian Government sets up a reciprocal tariff, this fine healthy industry is doomed to a struggle against adverse circumstances, and the prosperity of Canada will be retarded.
Our neighbours to the south have a great advantage over us in that their season is two or three weeks earlier than ours in respect to all produce; that gives them the 23)
opportunity of getting the first market, and the first market is always the best. I submit seriously to the government that something ought to be done on this subject of tariff. At least they should consider doing something, but evidently they are not considering doing anything. If they wish to do right by the people of this country, if they have any interest in their welfare, it seems to me that they should consider what action should be taken in this respect. I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) who said it appeared to him that in dealing with our friends on the other side of the line retaliation was the proper medicine.
I have no doubt that hon. members particularly to my left would be greatly disappointed if I did not mention the oriental question. There is just a chance, you know, that unless we say something the government will come to the conclusion that the oriental question is a dead issue. But it is not a dead issue by any means; the people of British Columbia are not going to let it die. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) knows what it is. I was sorry to see him leave the Department of Immigration. I do not know whether we shall have as good a friend in the present minister; he may be all right, but some of the statements he made in the House-in dealing with this subject, about the business we would lose and that kind of thing did not appeal to me at all. It is not a matter of business; it is a matter of the future of this country. If we do not get any business at all from Japan it does not make any difference to us. They have got to do the business anyway; they are buying these things from us because they think it pays them to do so. So that from what the present Minister of Immigration (Mr. Robb) has said on several occasions, it seems to me that he is making too much of that point. Let us forget that business question altogether and think about the matter from the point of view of nationality. As I say, the people of British Columbia are not allowing this oriental question to die; far from it. They are starting something, and the government should be in on it-an oriental survey of the whole Pacific coast, which has opened in the city of Vancouver under the direction of Dr. Robert E. Park of the University of Chicago. If the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Robb) were here I would ask him to pay particular attention to what I am about to read. This is from an article in the Vancouver Province of recent date:

The Address-Mr. McQuarrie
The survey in question will be both scientific and comprehensive. The oriental problem on this coast resembles the weather, of which Mark Twain complained "that though everyone had talked about it very little had been done." The aim of the survey is to replace opinion with facts. For this purpose a carefully directed study will be devoted for a year or more to every phase of the relationship of the oriental to this continent. The survey, in consequence, will not concern itself with any viewpoint or the support or advocacy of any school of thought on this subject.
It is also felt that so far as the oriental is concerned the Pacific slope of Canada and the United States is the racial frontier of America.
The institute offered to co-operate with the people of the coast on any plan for an exhaustive and scientific study of the matter. As a result regional councils have been formed at five points-Vancouver, Seattle, Portland, San Francisco and Los Angeles, and groups at these points have undertaken to raise $30,000 for the work of the survey. The Institute of Social and Religious Research is contributing $25,000.
For this work, the co-operation of the University of Chicago had to be enlisted, as Dr. Park, who is one of the outstanding sociological and psychological experts of America, had to be released for this special work for a year at least. He is the author of a number of works on racial studies made among the negroes of the South, and the Poles, Hebrews and European immigrants. He adopts original and unstereotyped methods. "Get experience, not opinions", he says, "for human experiences are more valuable than statistics. Back of every opinion is an experience. These experiences may not justify opinions, but they explain them."
There will be some very eminent men on the executive. It is under the chairmanship of Dr. Wilbur, head of Leland Stanford University, and includes among its members Dr. Boggs, of the University of British Columbia, Professor Mackenzie of the University of Washington, Professor Sissons of Reed College, Portland, Dr. Bird, President of Occidental College, Los Angeles, and Mr. Mc-Caughey, for fifteen years Superintendent of Education in the Hawaiian Islands.
This survey is going to be most important, and I would suggest to the Minister of Immigration and to the government that the government should take some part in it. So far as I am concerned experience as well as opinion has convinced me that we shall eventually have to come to exclusion; nothing short of that will do. I understand that in the United States also they are contemplating exclusion against the Japanese as well as against the Chinese. During the debate of last session the Prime Minister called attention to the fact that no country in the world had exclusion against the Japanese. If exclusion becomes law in the United States, will the Prime Minister of this country think it is time to have exclusion here? If we are going to have exclusion eventually, now is the time to commence, before this country is filled up with these orientals.

I would also submit, Mr. Speaker, with all due deference, that the gentleman's agreement which was negotiated by your worthy self in Japan a number of years ago has outlived its usefulness. It may have been the best arrangement that could have been made at that time, but I submit that the time has come when we in this country should control our own immigration without reference to any foreign country whether friendly or unfriendly. I submit that the gentleman's agreement should be immediately cancelled. Let us make our own immigration laws.
There is just one other matter I shall touch on. The Japanese treaty should be abrogated, for this reason, that it prevents us from passing provincial legislation as to the holding of land and other matters in connection with property and civil rights, and the result is that the most valuable land in British Columbia in the cities and in the country is being acquired by the orientals. My good friends who have been out there know that to be the case. They know that the oriental is taking firm hold and deep root in British Columbia. We must stop it. We cannot stop it by provincial legislation so long as that treaty exists, and I say that if we are going to keep this a white man's country, which it should be, if we are going to keep it for our children and our children's children, now is the time to take action.
